name: ATMEGA1284P-AU
title: ATmega164A/164PA/324A/324PA/644A/644PA/1284/1284P: 8-bit AVR microcontrollers with 16 to 128 Kbytes of in-system programmable Flash, 1.8 V to 5.5 V
summary: A family of 8-bit AVR RISC microcontrollers that runs most of its 131 instructions in one clock, giving close to 1 MIPS per MHz up to 20 MHz, from a 1.8 V to 5.5 V supply. The ATmega1284P carries 128 Kbytes of self-programmable Flash with a read-while-write boot section, 16 Kbytes of SRAM and 4 Kbytes of EEPROM, 32 I/O lines, two USARTs, SPI, a two-wire serial interface, an 8-channel 10-bit ADC, four timer/counters, JTAG with on-chip debug and six sleep modes. The smaller members share the pinout with 16, 32 or 64 Kbytes of Flash.
key_figures: 8-bit AVR, 131 instructions, 32 × 8-bit working registers, up to 20 MIPS at 20 MHz
0.6 µA with the 32 kHz RTC running, 1.8 V, 25 °C

circuits.title: Crystal or ceramic resonator on XTAL1/XTAL2
circuits.description: A quartz crystal or ceramic resonator between XTAL1 and XTAL2 runs the on-chip inverting amplifier as the system oscillator, with one capacitor from each pin to ground. C1 and C2 are always equal. Their best value depends on the crystal, the stray capacitance and the noise around the board; 12 pF to 22 pF is the recommended range for crystals in both crystal oscillator modes, and a ceramic resonator takes the values its maker gives.

circuits.title: 32.768 kHz watch crystal on TOSC1/TOSC2
circuits.description: A 32.768 kHz watch crystal straight across TOSC1 (PC6) and TOSC2 (PC7) clocks Timer/Counter2 as a real-time counter, which keeps running in Power-save. The timer oscillator puts 6 pF on each pin; a crystal rated for a higher load than that needs external capacitors from each pin to ground, as in the XTAL crystal circuit, sized by Ce + Ci = 2·CL − Cs. The crystal's ESR should be at most 65 kΩ for 9 pF and 30 kΩ for 12.5 pF load.

circuits.title: External clock drive
circuits.description: An external clock of 0 MHz to 20 MHz drives XTAL1 with CKSEL = 0000; XTAL2 is left unconnected. The frequency must not step by more than 2 % from one cycle to the next; larger changes are made with the part held in reset, or with the system clock prescaler.

circuits.title: TWI bus with pull-up resistors
circuits.description: Two-wire bus: the ATmega1284P's SCL (PC0) and SDA (PC1) join the same two lines of every other device on the bus, and one resistor on each line pulls it to VCC. All drivers are open-drain, so the bus is a wired-AND: any device pulls a line low, and the resistor brings it high when all let go. The pull-up value follows from the SCL frequency and the bus capacitance, which may total at most 400 pF.

parts.note: any further devices on the bus connect the same way

circuits.title: ADC power connections
circuits.description: AVCC is fed from the digital VCC through a 10 µH inductor, with a 100 nF capacitor from AVCC to ground forming an LC filter that keeps digital supply noise out of the ADC. The ADC pins (PA0 to PA7), AREF, AVCC and the filter sit over an analog ground plane.

circuits.title: Parallel programming connections
circuits.description: The pins a high-voltage parallel programmer drives. VCC and AVCC take +5 V and GND is ground. RESET takes +12 V to enter programming mode. PD1 reports ready/busy back to the programmer; PD2 to PD7 and PA0 take OE, WR, BS1, XA0, XA1, PAGEL and BS2. PB0 to PB7 form the bidirectional data bus, and XTAL1 receives the pulses that load addresses, data and commands. Every other pin is left floating.
notes: Unused pins are left floating.

circuits.title: Serial programming and verify connections
circuits.description: In-system serial programming: VCC and AVCC take 1.8 to 5.5 V, with AVCC within 0.3 V of VCC. The programmer drives MOSI (PB5) and SCK (PB7), reads MISO (PB6), and holds RESET low for the session. A clock source drives XTAL1 unless the part runs from its internal oscillator.

operation.text: Low-power CMOS 8-bit microcontrollers on the AVR enhanced RISC core. With most instructions done in one clock, throughput nears 1 MIPS per MHz, so clock speed can be traded directly against current.

The 32 working registers all connect to the ALU, so one instruction can take two independent registers and finish in one clock. Beside the memories the chips carry an RTC, three timer/counters with compare and PWM (four on ATmega1284/1284P), two USARTs, a byte-oriented two-wire interface, SPI, an 8-channel 10-bit ADC with an optional differential input stage and programmable gain, a watchdog with its own oscillator, JTAG (IEEE 1149.1) for test, debug and programming, and six software-selected power-saving modes.

Idle stops the CPU while SRAM, timers, SPI and interrupts keep working. Power-down keeps register contents but stops the oscillator and everything else until an interrupt or hardware reset. Power-save leaves the asynchronous timer running as a time base. ADC Noise Reduction stops the CPU and all I/O except the asynchronous timer and the ADC. Standby keeps the crystal or resonator oscillator running for a very fast start-up; Extended Standby keeps both it and the asynchronous timer running.

The Flash can be rewritten in the system over SPI, by a conventional non-volatile memory programmer, or by a boot program running on the core, which may load the application over any interface. Code in the boot section keeps running while the application section is written: true read-while-write.

Ports A to D are 8-bit bidirectional ports with a pull-up selectable per bit and symmetrical drive, strong in both sink and source. An input with its pull-up on sources current when pulled low from outside. All port pins go tri-state as soon as a reset starts, clock or no clock. Port A also carries the ADC inputs and is supplied from AVCC; Port C carries the JTAG interface.
Projected retention failures, from qualification, stay far below 1 PPM for 20 years at 85 °C, and likewise for 100 years at 25 °C.
The QTouch library adds touch buttons, sliders and wheels to the part in software, using QTouch or QMatrix acquisition; an API sets up the channels and sensors and reports their states.

Harvard architecture, where program and data each have their own memory and bus, with a one-level pipeline that fetches the next instruction while the current one runs, so an instruction completes every clock. The register file has 32 × 8-bit registers with single-cycle access: two operands are read, the ALU works and the result is written back in one clock. Six registers pair up as the 16-bit X, Y and Z pointers for indirect data addressing; Z also points into Flash for table look-up.

Jumps and calls reach the whole address space. Most instructions are one 16-bit word; every program address holds a 16- or 32-bit instruction. The Flash divides into a boot program section and an application section, each with lock bits against write and read/write; the SPM instruction that writes the application section must run from the boot section. Return addresses go on a stack in general SRAM, so its size is bounded only by the SRAM; software must set SP in the reset routine before any call or interrupt. Five addressing modes reach the SRAM.

Every interrupt has its own vector and its own enable bit, plus the global enable in the status register; a lower vector address means higher priority. The I/O space has 64 addresses, reached directly or as data addresses 0x20-0x5F; the extended I/O space 0x60-0xFF in SRAM is reached only with ST/STS/STD and LD/LDS/LDD.

The ALU does arithmetic, logic and bit operations between registers or between a register and a constant in one clock, and includes a signed/unsigned multiplier with fractional format. The status register reflects the result of the last arithmetic instruction, which often removes the need for a separate compare. It is not saved on entry to an interrupt or restored on return; software does that.

The register file supports one 8-bit operand in with an 8-bit result, two 8-bit operands with an 8-bit result, two 8-bit operands with a 16-bit result, and one 16-bit operand with a 16-bit result. Most instructions on it reach every register in a single cycle. The registers also sit at data addresses 0x00-0x1F (R0 at 0x00 up to R31 at 0x1F), so the X, Y and Z pointers can index any of them.
R26/R27 form X, R28/R29 form Y and R30/R31 form Z, low byte first. In the addressing modes they serve as fixed displacement, auto-increment and auto-decrement pointers.

The stack grows downward from high memory, and a PUSH decrements SP. It must be placed in SRAM by the program before any call or interrupt is enabled; SP starts at the last SRAM address and must point above the start of SRAM. SP is two 8-bit I/O registers, SPH and SPL, of which the device uses 11 to 14 bits.
On the ATmega1284/1284P, ELPM and SPM address Flash with a 24-bit Z made from RAMPZ, ZH and ZL; LPM ignores RAMPZ. Unused RAMPZ bits read zero and should be written zero.

The CPU runs from clkCPU, taken straight from the selected clock source with no internal division. Instruction fetch overlaps execution, and a two-register ALU operation with write-back completes in one clock, for up to 1 MIPS per MHz.

The lowest program addresses hold the reset and interrupt vectors by default; RESET has top priority, then INT0. IVSEL in MCUCR moves the vectors to the start of the boot section, and the BOOTRST fuse moves the reset vector there. With boot lock bits BLB02 or BLB12 programmed, interrupts may be blocked depending on where the program counter is. Entering an interrupt clears the global I-bit; software may set it again to allow nesting, and RETI sets it. Flag-type interrupts are remembered while disabled and run in priority order once enabled, and hardware clears the flag on entry (or software writes one to clear it). Level-type interrupts last only while the condition is present and may have no flag. After return one more main-program instruction runs before any pending interrupt. CLI takes effect at once, even for an interrupt arriving in the same cycle; the instruction after SEI runs before any pending interrupt.

At least four clocks pass from an interrupt to the first instruction of its vector, while the program counter is pushed; the usual jump to the handler takes three more. A multi-cycle instruction in progress finishes first. Waking from sleep adds four clocks on top of the sleep mode's start-up time. RETI takes four clocks: the 3-byte program counter is popped, SP rises by two and the I-bit is set.
Two main spaces, data and program, plus a separate EEPROM; all three are linear.

16/32/64/128 Kbytes, organized in 16-bit words because every instruction is 16 or 32 bits, and split into a boot section and an application section for software security. Endurance is at least 10,000 write/erase cycles. Constant tables can sit anywhere in program memory and are read with LPM.

The data space starts with the 32 registers, then 64 standard I/O registers, then 160 extended I/O registers, then the internal SRAM (1024/2048/4096/16384 bytes) from 0x0100. Addressing modes are direct (whole data space), indirect with displacement (63 locations from Y or Z), plain indirect, and indirect with pre-decrement or post-increment of the pointer; all of them reach the registers, I/O and SRAM.
An internal SRAM access takes two clkCPU cycles.

512/1K/2K/4K bytes in a separate data space, read and written a byte at a time, with at least 100,000 write/erase cycles. Its address, data and control registers are in I/O space. A self-timing function lets software see when the next byte can be written, and a set write procedure guards against accidental writes. A read halts the CPU for four clocks and a write for two before the next instruction.

At too low a VCC an EEPROM write can fail and the CPU can misexecute, so either can corrupt data. Holding the part in reset while the supply is too low prevents it: use the internal brown-out detector, or an external low-VCC reset circuit where the BOD level does not fit. A write in progress when reset arrives completes, provided the supply is high enough.

All I/O and peripheral registers lie in the I/O space. LD/LDS/LDD and ST/STS/STD reach all of it; IN and OUT use I/O addresses 0x00-0x3F, and LD/ST add 0x20 to those. Registers at 0x00-0x1F are bit-addressable with SBI and CBI and testable with SBIS and SBIC; on this part SBI and CBI touch only the named bit, so they are safe on registers whose flags clear by writing one. Reserved bits should be written zero and reserved addresses never written. Three general purpose I/O registers hold any data, such as global variables and flags.

Not all clocks need run at once; sleep modes stop the ones not in use. clkCPU runs the core (register file, status register, stack memory). clkI/O runs most peripherals such as the timers, SPI and USART, and the external interrupt module, though some external interrupts are detected asynchronously with clkI/O stopped, and TWI address recognition works in every sleep mode. clkFLASH runs the Flash interface, normally together with clkCPU. clkASY lets the asynchronous timer run from an external clock or 32 kHz crystal, so it can count real time in sleep. clkADC is a separate domain, so the CPU and I/O clocks can stop during a conversion to cut digital noise.

The clock source is chosen by Flash fuse bits (CKSEL) among six: a crystal oscillator in low-power or full-swing form, a 32 kHz low-frequency crystal oscillator, an internal 128 kHz RC, the calibrated internal RC, or a clock applied from outside.

Parts ship running from the internal RC oscillator at 8.0 MHz with CKDIV8 programmed, so the system clock is 1.0 MHz, with the longest start-up and the time-out enabled (CKSEL = 0010, SUT = 10, CKDIV8 = 0). This lets any programming interface reach the part to set the clock wanted.

After every other reset source releases, an internal reset holds for a time-out tTOUT counted on the watchdog oscillator; SUT and CKSEL set its length (0, 512 or 8K cycles). Its job is to wait for VCC to reach the minimum, but it does not watch the voltage, so it must be longer than the VCC rise time; if that cannot be met, use the internal or an external brown-out detector, which allows the time-out to be dropped. Dropping the time-out without a BOD is not recommended. A ripple counter then holds reset for a number of oscillator cycles so the clock can settle, from 6 cycles for an external clock to 32K for a low-frequency crystal. From reset both delays apply; waking from Power-save or Power-down only the oscillator start-up applies.
XTAL1 and XTAL2 are the input and output of an inverting amplifier that runs a quartz crystal or ceramic resonator. C1 and C2 are always equal for both.

Reduced swing on XTAL2 gives the lowest current, but it cannot drive other clock inputs and is more open to noise. CKSEL3..1 picks one of three modes by frequency range, and CKSEL0 with SUT1..0 picks the start-up time.
Rail-to-rail swing on XTAL2 suits driving other clock inputs and noisy surroundings, at a higher current than the low power oscillator. It works only with VCC from 2.7 V to 5.5 V.

Made for a 32.768 kHz watch crystal and tuned for very low current, so the crystal's load capacitance and ESR both matter (ESR at most 65 kΩ at 9 pF, 30 kΩ at 12.5 pF). Each TOSC pin carries an internal load capacitance; a crystal specifying a higher CL needs external capacitors, as with the main crystal. SUT and CKSEL0 set the start-up time.

About 8 MHz by default; it varies with voltage and temperature but can be calibrated closely. At reset hardware loads the factory calibration byte into OSCCAL; software may write OSCCAL for better accuracy. It needs no external parts. The watchdog oscillator still clocks the watchdog and the reset time-out when the RC oscillator runs the chip. SUT sets the start-up time.
A low-power 128 kHz oscillator, nominal at 3 V and 25 °C, selected with CKSEL = 0011; SUT sets the start-up time.

XTAL1 is driven by an external clock with CKSEL = 0000; XTAL2 is left open. The applied frequency must change smoothly: more than 2 % from one cycle to the next can cause unpredictable behaviour, so larger changes are made with the part held in reset. The system clock prescaler gives safe run-time frequency changes.

The timer oscillator is the same design as the low frequency crystal oscillator. Timer/Counter2 can run from a 32.768 kHz watch crystal on TOSC1/TOSC2 or from an external clock on TOSC1, chosen with EXTCLK in ASSR.

With the CKOUT fuse programmed, the system clock appears on CLKO (PB1), including during reset, overriding the pin's normal I/O use. Any clock source can be output; with the prescaler in use the divided clock is output.

CLKPR divides the system clock to save current when less speed is needed; it works with every clock source and divides clkI/O, clkADC, clkCPU and clkFLASH. Changing the setting gives no glitches and no intermediate frequency above the old or new one. The prescaler state cannot be read and the exact switch time cannot be predicted. To change CLKPS, write CLKPCE to one with all other CLKPR bits zero, then within four cycles write the new CLKPS with CLKPCE zero, with interrupts disabled throughout.

Sleep modes stop unused modules to save power; the BOD keeps watching the supply during sleep when enabled, and on the PA and 1284P parts can be turned off by software in some modes. Setting SE in SMCR and executing SLEEP enters the mode chosen by SM2..0. An enabled interrupt wakes the MCU, which halts four cycles beyond the start-up time, runs the interrupt routine and continues after the SLEEP instruction. Register file and SRAM survive sleep. A reset during sleep wakes the part to the reset vector.

On the ATmega164PA/324PA/644PA/1284P, software can turn the brown-out detector off during Power-down, Power-save, Standby and Extended Standby by writing BODS (bit 6 of MCUCR) through a timed sequence with an enable bit, bringing sleep current down to the level with the BOD fuse-disabled. The BOD switches off right after sleep starts and back on at wake-up; waking then takes about 60 µs so the BOD is working before code resumes. BODS = 0, the default, keeps the BOD on.

SM2..0 = 000. The CPU and Flash clocks stop; SPI, USART, analog comparator, ADC, two-wire interface, timers, watchdog and interrupts carry on. Both external and internal interrupts (timer overflow, USART transmit complete) wake it. Setting ACD in ACSR powers the comparator down to save more if its interrupt is not needed. An enabled ADC starts a conversion on entry.

SM2..0 = 001. clkI/O, clkCPU and clkFLASH stop; the ADC, external interrupts, TWI address match, Timer/Counter2 and watchdog carry on if enabled, giving a quieter supply for higher ADC resolution. An enabled ADC starts a conversion on entry. Wake-up sources: ADC conversion complete, external reset, watchdog reset or interrupt, brown-out reset, a TWI interrupt, a Timer/Counter2 interrupt, SPM/EEPROM ready, an external level interrupt or a pin change interrupt.

SM2..0 = 010. The external oscillator stops; external interrupts, the two-wire interface and the watchdog carry on if enabled, so only asynchronous modules work. Wake-up comes only from an external reset, watchdog reset, brown-out reset, TWI address match, an INT2:0 interrupt or a pin change interrupt. A level interrupt used for wake-up must be held for some time. The wake-up delay, while the clock restarts and settles, is set by the same CKSEL fuses as the reset time-out.

SM2..0 = 011. Like Power-down, except that an enabled Timer/Counter2 keeps running and its overflow or compare match wakes the part when its TIMSK2 bits and the global I-bit are set. With Timer/Counter2 stopped, Power-down suits better. Timer/Counter2 may be clocked synchronously or asynchronously in this mode; whichever clock it does not use is stopped, and the synchronous clock serves only Timer/Counter2.

With an external crystal or resonator selected, SM2..0 = 110 gives Standby, which is Power-down with the oscillator left running, and 111 gives Extended Standby, which is Power-save with the oscillator left running. Both wake in six clock cycles.

PRR stops the clock to single peripherals. The stopped peripheral freezes, its registers cannot be read or written, and the resources it holds stay taken, so it should normally be disabled first. Clearing its PRR bit brings it back in the state it was left. It saves power in Active and Idle; in the other sleep modes the clocks are already stopped.

Use sleep as much as possible, in the deepest mode that still serves, and turn off what is not needed. An enabled ADC stays enabled in every sleep mode, so disable it first; the next conversion after re-enabling is an extended one. Disable the analog comparator in Idle when unused and in ADC Noise Reduction always; in other modes it turns off by itself, unless it uses the internal reference, in which case disable it in every mode. A fuse-enabled BOD and an enabled watchdog run in every sleep mode and add markedly to deep-sleep current. The internal reference is on whenever the BOD, comparator or ADC needs it and must be given its start-up time after being turned back on.

No pin should drive a resistive load in sleep. In modes where clkI/O and clkADC both stop, the digital input buffers are disabled except where needed for wake-up. A floating input or one near VCC/2 makes an enabled buffer draw excess current, so analog inputs should always have their digital buffer turned off with DIDR1 and DIDR0, even in active mode.
With OCDEN programmed the main clock stays on in sleep and adds markedly to deep-sleep current. The OCD system is turned off by unprogramming OCDEN or JTAGEN, or by writing one to JTD in MCUCR.

During reset all I/O registers take their initial values and execution starts at the reset vector, which must hold a JMP to the reset routine. Unused interrupt vectors may hold ordinary code, also when the reset and interrupt vectors are in different sections. I/O ports go to their initial state as soon as a reset source is active, with no clock needed. When all sources have released, a delay counter set by SUT and CKSEL stretches the internal reset so the supply can settle.

Five: power-on reset while the supply is below VPOT; external reset from a low on R̅E̅S̅E̅T̅ longer than the minimum pulse; watchdog reset when an enabled watchdog times out; brown-out reset while VCC is below VBOT with the BOD enabled; and JTAG AVR reset for as long as a one sits in the JTAG reset register. MCUSR records which source caused the reset (PORF, BORF, EXTRF, WDRF, JTRF).

An on-chip detector issues the power-on reset whenever VCC is below its detection level, both at start-up and on a supply failure. Reaching the threshold starts the delay counter that sets how long reset is held after VCC rises; reset returns at once, with no delay, when VCC falls below the level. R̅E̅S̅E̅T̅ may be tied to VCC, or held low externally to extend the start-up.

A low on R̅E̅S̅E̅T̅ longer than the minimum pulse width resets the part even with no clock; shorter pulses may not. When the pin rises past the reset threshold VRST, the delay counter starts the MCU after tTOUT. The pin has an internal pull-up and a spike filter.

An on-chip BOD compares VCC with a fixed level chosen by the BODLEVEL fuses, with hysteresis against spikes. Falling below VBOT- asserts reset at once; rising above VBOT+ starts the delay counter, which releases the MCU after tTOUT. A dip is only caught if it stays below the level longer than tBOD.
A watchdog time-out produces a one-CK reset pulse; its falling edge starts the tTOUT delay.

An internal bandgap reference serves the BOD and can feed the analog comparator or the ADC. It is on only when the BOD is enabled by BODLEVEL, when ACBG connects it to the comparator, or when the ADC is enabled; without the BOD, software must wait out its start-up time after setting ACBG or enabling the ADC before using their results. Avoiding all three before Power-down turns it off and saves current.

The watchdog counts cycles of its own 128 kHz on-chip oscillator, with time-outs selectable from 16 ms to 8 s (2K to 1024K oscillator cycles, WDP3..0). Software restarts it with WDR before the time-out. Interrupt mode gives an interrupt, usable for wake-up or as a general timer; System Reset mode resets the part against runaway code; Interrupt and System Reset mode first interrupts, for example to save data, then switches to reset. The WDTON fuse forces System Reset mode with WDE locked to 1 and WDIE to 0.

To clear WDE or change the time-out: in one operation write ones to WDCE and WDE (WDE must be written one whatever it held); then within four clock cycles, in one operation, write WDE and WDP as wanted with WDCE zero. Interrupts should be kept from running during the sequence. Reset the watchdog before changing WDP, because switching to a shorter period can cause an immediate time-out.

A watchdog enabled by accident, by a runaway pointer or a brown-out, resets the part and stays enabled, which can lead to endless time-out resets if the code does not expect it. Startup code should therefore always clear WDRF and WDE, even when the watchdog is not used.

The vector table starts at program address 0x0000 with the reset vector, and each following vector sits two addresses higher, up to 0x0044 for vector 35. Vectors 32 to 35 (Timer/Counter3) apply to the ATmega1284P only. With BOOTRST unprogrammed and IVSEL clear, reset is at 0x0000 and the interrupt vectors start at 0x0002; BOOTRST moves the reset address and IVSEL moves the interrupt vectors to the boot section.

IVSEL in MCUCR places the vectors at the start of Flash (0) or at the start of the boot loader section (1), whose address the BOOTSZ fuses set. To change IVSEL, write IVCE to one, then within four cycles write the new IVSEL with IVCE zero. Interrupts are disabled automatically from the cycle IVCE is set until after the instruction that follows the write to IVSEL.

INT2:0 and PCINT31:0 trigger interrupts even when the pins are outputs, which gives a way to make software interrupts. PCI3 fires on a toggle of any enabled PCINT31:24 pin, PCI2 on PCINT23:16, PCI1 on PCINT15:8 and PCI0 on PCINT7:0; PCMSK3..0 pick the contributing pins. Pin change interrupts are detected asynchronously and can wake the part from sleep modes beyond Idle, but they need an active I/O clock to be generated, so in deeper sleep the pin must stay toggled until the part is fully awake or the wake-up completes without an interrupt. INT2:0 can trigger on a low level or on either edge, as set in EICRA; a low-level interrupt repeats while the pin is held low. Level and edge detection on INT2:0 is asynchronous and works in all sleep modes. A level used to wake from Power-down must be held until the start-up time ends, or the part wakes without taking the interrupt.

Every port has true read-modify-write behaviour: SBI and CBI change one pin's direction, output value or pull-up without disturbing the others. Outputs drive symmetrically with high sink and source capability, enough for LED displays. Each pin has a pull-up whose resistance does not depend on the supply, and protection diodes to VCC and ground. Each port has three I/O addresses: PORTx (data, read/write), DDRx (direction, read/write) and PINx (input, read only). PUD in MCUCR turns off every pull-up on every port. Enabling an alternate function on some pins leaves the rest of the port usable as general I/O.

DDxn = 1 makes Pxn an output and 0 an input. As an input, PORTxn = 1 turns the pull-up on; writing PORTxn zero or making the pin an output turns it off. As an output, PORTxn sets the level driven. Pins go tri-state when a reset is active, even with no clock.
Writing one to a PINxn bit toggles PORTxn, whatever DDxn holds; SBI can toggle a single bit.

A change from tri-state (DDxn, PORTxn = 00) to output high (11), or back, passes through either pull-up on (01) or output low (10). Pull-up on is normally harmless; if not, PUD can turn off all pull-ups. A change from pulled-up input to output low, or back, has the same issue, and tri-state or output high should be used as the step in the middle.

PINxn reads the pin whatever the direction, through a latch and register that form a synchronizer against metastability. A change on the pin reaches PINxn after between ½ and 1½ system clocks depending on when it arrives. Reading back a value just written by software needs a nop between the out and the in, giving a delay of one clock.

In Power-down, Power-save and Standby the sleep controller clamps each digital input to ground ahead of its Schmitt trigger, so floating or mid-level inputs do not draw excess current. The clamp is lifted for pins enabled as external interrupts and by some alternate functions. If an asynchronous external interrupt pin set for rising edge, falling edge or any change sits high while that interrupt is not enabled, its flag will be set on leaving those modes, since the clamp release looks like a change.

Unused pins should be held at a defined level to avoid extra current in Reset, Active and Idle, where the inputs are live. The internal pull-up is the simplest choice, though it is off during reset; where current during reset matters, an external resistor to either rail does the job. Wiring a pin straight to a supply rail is advised against, because the pin draws excess current should it ever be made an output.

Most pins have alternate functions besides general I/O. The module owning an alternate function can override the pin's pull-up, output driver enable, output value, toggle and digital input enable through override-enable and override-value signals; it reads the pin through the digital input DI and analog signals through AIO, which connects straight to the pad. The signals WRx, WPx, WDx, RRx, RPx and RDx serve a whole port; clkI/O, SLEEP and PUD are shared across all ports; the override signals are per pin.

SCK, MISO, MOSI and S̅S̅: the SPI forces an input where its role needs one (SCK, MOSI and S̅S̅ as slave, MISO as master) and otherwise leaves the direction to DDB; a forced input keeps its pull-up control through PORTB. As slave, the SPI is active while S̅S̅ is low. Compare outputs OC0A, OC0B, OC3A and OC3B need the pin set as an output and also serve as PWM outputs. CLKO on PB1 overrides PORTB1 and DDB1 when CKOUT is programmed and also runs during reset. XCK0 on PB0 is output or input according to its DDR bit and works only with USART0 in synchronous mode.

Compare outputs OC2A, OC2B, OC1A and OC1B need the pin set as an output and also serve as PWM outputs. TXD0 and TXD1 become outputs whenever their transmitter is enabled; RXD0 and RXD1 become inputs whenever their receiver is enabled, with the pull-up still under PORTD control. XCK1 on PD4 is output or input by DDD4 and works only with USART1 in synchronous mode. T3 on PD0 exists only on the ATmega1284/1284P.

An 8-bit timer/counter with two output compare units, each with a double-buffered compare register and its own pin (OC0A, OC0B). It offers clear-on-compare (auto reload), a variable-period glitch-free phase correct PWM, fast PWM and a frequency generator, and three interrupt sources: overflow TOV0 and compare matches OCF0A and OCF0B. Flags sit in TIFR0 and each interrupt has its own mask bit in TIMSK0. TCNT0, OCR0A and OCR0B are 8-bit registers.

The counter runs from the internal clock through the prescaler or from an external clock on the T0 pin; CS02:0 in TCCR0B pick the source and edge. With CS02:0 = 0 no clock is selected and the counter stands still, though the CPU can still read and write TCNT0. The selected clock is called clkT0. A CPU write to TCNT0 takes priority over a clear or count in the same cycle.

WGM01:0 in TCCR0A and WGM02 in TCCR0B set the count sequence and with it how the compare outputs behave; the overflow flag TOV0 is set at the point the selected mode defines and can raise an interrupt. Depending on the mode the counter is cleared, counts up or counts down on each clkT0.

TCNT0 is compared with OCR0A and OCR0B on every timer clock. A match sets OCF0A or OCF0B on the next timer clock, raising an interrupt when enabled; the flag clears when the interrupt runs or when a one is written to it. The waveform generator turns matches into pin activity according to WGM02:0 and COM0x1:0. In the PWM modes OCR0x is double buffered and its new value is taken at TOP or BOTTOM so no odd-length pulse appears; in Normal and CTC modes the CPU writes OCR0x directly.

In the non-PWM modes writing one to FOC0x updates OC0x as a real match would (set, clear or toggle per COM0x1:0) without setting OCF0x or clearing the counter. Any CPU write to TCNT0 blocks a compare match in the following timer clock, even with the timer stopped, so OCR0x can be loaded with the same value as TCNT0 without an interrupt when the clock starts. Writing TCNT0 equal to OCR0x therefore loses that match, and writing BOTTOM while counting down should be avoided. Set OC0x up (most easily with FOC0x in Normal mode) before making the pin an output; OC0x holds its value across mode changes. COM0x1:0 are not double buffered and act at once.

When either COM0x1:0 bit is set, OC0x replaces the port's output value on its pin, but the pin only shows it once its DDR bit makes it an output. This override does not depend on the waveform mode. A system reset clears the internal OC0x register. A changed COM0x1:0 takes effect at the next compare match; in the non-PWM modes FOC0x makes it immediate. Some COM0x1:0 settings are reserved in some modes.

WGM02:0 = 0. The counter only counts up, passes 0xFF and starts again at 0x00, with no clear. TOV0 is set in the timer clock in which TCNT0 becomes zero and behaves like a ninth bit that is only ever set; with the overflow interrupt clearing it, software can extend the count. TCNT0 can be written at any time. The compare unit can time interrupts; making waveforms with it in this mode takes too much CPU time.

WGM02:0 = 2. The counter clears to zero when TCNT0 matches OCR0A, so OCR0A sets TOP and the resolution; this gives fine control of the output frequency and makes external event counting simpler. OCF0A can interrupt at every TOP and the handler may change TOP, but this mode has no double buffering: writing an OCR0A below the current count makes the counter run on to 0xFF and wrap before the next match. With COM0A1:0 = 1, OC0A toggles on every match; the highest frequency is fclk_I/O/2, with OCR0A = 0. TOV0 is set when the counter passes from MAX to 0x00.

WGM02:0 = 3 (TOP = 0xFF) or 7 (TOP = OCR0A). Single slope: the counter runs from BOTTOM to TOP and restarts at BOTTOM in the next timer clock, so the PWM frequency can be twice that of the dual-slope phase correct mode, which suits power regulation, rectification and DAC uses and allows small inductors and capacitors. Non-inverting output (COM0x1:0 = 2) clears OC0x on the compare match and sets it at BOTTOM; inverting (3) does the reverse. With WGM02 set, COM0A1:0 = 1 toggles OC0A on each match; OC0B has no toggle option. TOV0 is set at TOP and its interrupt can be used to load a new compare value. OCR0A = BOTTOM gives a narrow spike every MAX+1 timer clocks; OCR0A = MAX gives a steady high or low depending on COM0A1:0. A 50 % square wave of up to fclk_I/O/2 comes from toggling OC0x with OCR0A = 0, like CTC toggling but with double-buffered compare values.

WGM02:0 = 1 (TOP = 0xFF) or 5 (TOP = OCR0A). Dual slope: the counter runs up from BOTTOM to TOP and back down, holding TOP for one timer clock. Non-inverting output clears OC0x on the match while counting up and sets it on the match while counting down; inverting output is the reverse. The top frequency is lower than single slope, but the symmetric waveform suits motor control. TOV0 is set at BOTTOM. With WGM02 set, COM0A0 = 1 toggles OC0A on matches; not available for OC0B. With non-inverted output OCR0A = BOTTOM holds the output low and OCR0A = MAX holds it high; inverted output is the opposite. To keep the output symmetric about BOTTOM, OC0x can change at the start of a period without a match: when OCR0A moves away from MAX, and when the timer starts from a count above OCR0A and so misses the match on the way up.

The timer is synchronous: clkT0 acts as a clock enable on clkI/O. TOV0 is set as the count passes from MAX to BOTTOM in the modes other than phase correct PWM, and OCF0x is set one timer clock after TCNT0 equals OCR0x (OCF0B in every mode, OCF0A in all but those where OCR0A is TOP). In CTC and in fast PWM with OCR0A as TOP, OCF0A is set and TCNT0 cleared as the count leaves TOP. With the prescaler, these events line up with the prescaled timer clock (for example fclk_I/O/8).

16-bit timer/counters (Timer/Counter3 on the ATmega1284 and 1284P only). Each has two output compare units with double-buffered compare registers, one input capture unit with a noise canceler, clear-on-compare, glitch-free phase correct PWM with a variable period, a frequency generator, an external event counter and four interrupt sources (TOVn, OCFnA, OCFnB, ICFn). PRTIM1 in PRR0 must be zero for Timer/Counter1 to run. TCNTn, OCRnA/B and ICRn are 16-bit registers; TCCRnA/B/C are 8-bit with no access restrictions. Flags are in TIFRn and masks in TIMSKn.

In some modes TOP comes from OCRnA, from ICRn or from a set of fixed values. With OCRnA as TOP in a PWM mode, OCRnA cannot drive a PWM output, but TOP is then double buffered and can change at run time. Where a fixed TOP is wanted, ICRn can hold it and leave OCRnA free for a PWM output. The input capture register can record the count on an edge at the ICPn pin or from the analog comparator, through a noise canceler.

The CPU reaches TCNTn, OCRnA/B and ICRn one byte at a time over the 8-bit bus. Each 16-bit timer has one 8-bit TEMP register for the high byte, shared by all its 16-bit registers; the low-byte access triggers the transfer. On a write, the high byte is written first into TEMP, and writing the low byte copies both bytes in the same clock. On a read, reading the low byte copies the high byte into TEMP in the same clock, and the high byte is read next. Reading OCRnA/B does not go through TEMP. In C the compiler orders the bytes. Registers in the extended I/O space need LDS/STS (with SBRS, SBRC, SBR, CBR) in place of IN, OUT, SBIS, SBIC, CBI and SBI.

A 16-bit access is two instructions. If an interrupt between them touches any 16-bit register of the same timer, it overwrites TEMP and corrupts the access outside the interrupt. When both main code and interrupt code use these registers, the main code must disable interrupts around each 16-bit access: save SREG, clear the global interrupt flag, do the two byte accesses, restore SREG. When several 16-bit registers are written with the same high byte, the high byte need be written only once, under the same atomicity rule.

CSn2:0 in TCCRnB select the internal prescaled clock or the external Tn pin. The prescaler runs freely, independent of the timer's clock select, and is shared by Timer/Counter1 and Timer/Counter0. Because of this, when a timer is started on a prescaled clock the first count comes 1 to N+1 system clocks later, N being the divisor (8, 64, 256 or 1024). A prescaler reset can synchronise a timer to program execution, but it changes the prescaler period for every timer connected to it.

TCNTn occupies two I/O bytes, TCNTnH and TCNTnL. The CPU reaches TCNTnH only through TEMP, which is loaded from TCNTnH when TCNTnL is read and copied to TCNTnH when TCNTnL is written, so the whole count moves in one clock. Some writes to TCNTn while counting give unpredictable results; they are noted with the modes concerned. CSn2:0 = 0 stops the timer but leaves TCNTn accessible; a CPU write wins over a clear or count. WGMn3:0 in TCCRnA and TCCRnB set the count sequence, and TOVn is set according to the mode.

On an edge at ICPn, or at the analog comparator output ACO, that matches the edge detector's setting, the 16-bit TCNTn is copied into ICRn and ICFn is set in the same system clock; with ICIEn = 1 an interrupt follows. ICFn clears when the interrupt runs or when one is written to it. Read ICRnL first, then ICRnH (through TEMP). ICRn can be written only in modes that use it as TOP; set WGMn3:0 first, then write ICRnH before ICRnL. The time stamps serve to measure frequency or duty cycle or to log events.

ICPn is the main trigger. Timer/Counter1 can instead take the analog comparator output, selected by ACIC in ACSR; switching the source can itself cause a capture, so clear ICFn afterwards. ICPn and ACO are sampled and edge-detected the same way as the Tn pin. The noise canceler and edge detector inputs are always active, except in waveform modes that use ICRn as TOP. Software can trigger a capture by driving the ICPn port pin.

Enabled by ICNCn in TCCRnB. It needs four equal samples in a row before its output, which feeds the edge detector, changes, and so adds four system clocks of delay from the input change to the ICRn update. It runs on the system clock and is not affected by the prescaler.

ICRn must be read before the next event or it is overwritten, so read it as early as possible in the interrupt handler; the worst-case response depends on the longest handling time of the other interrupts. Changing TOP while capturing is not recommended. For duty cycle, change the trigger edge after each capture, as soon as ICRn has been read, then clear ICFn by writing one to it; for frequency alone, with an interrupt handler, ICFn need not be cleared. In Normal mode the interval between events must not exceed the counter's range; use the overflow interrupt or the prescaler to extend it.

TCNTn is compared with OCRnx continuously; a match sets OCFnx on the next timer clock and, with OCIEnx = 1, raises an interrupt. Unit A can also set TOP, which fixes the resolution and the period of the generated waveform. OCRnx is double buffered in all twelve PWM modes, updated at TOP or BOTTOM; in Normal and CTC modes the CPU writes it directly. OCRnx changes only when written, so it is not read through TEMP, though reading the low byte first is good practice. Writing goes through TEMP: high byte first, and the low-byte write moves both into the buffer or compare register in one system clock.

FOCnx forces a match in non-PWM modes, updating OCnx without setting OCFnx or clearing the timer. A CPU write to TCNTn blocks any match in the next timer clock, even when stopped. Writing TCNTn equal to OCRnx loses that match; in PWM modes with a variable TOP, writing TCNTn equal to TOP loses the TOP match and the counter runs on to 0xFFFF; avoid writing BOTTOM while counting down. Set OCnx (most easily with FOCnx in Normal mode) before making the pin an output. COMnx1:0 are not double buffered and act at once.

Setting either COMnx1:0 bit hands the pin's output value to OCnx; the DDR bit must still make the pin an output for it to appear. The override is mostly independent of the waveform mode, with exceptions in some modes. A system reset clears OCnx. The input capture unit ignores COMnx1:0. A new COMnx1:0 value acts at the next compare match, or at once through FOCnx in non-PWM modes.

WGMn3:0 = 0. The counter counts up, passes 0xFFFF and restarts at 0x0000. TOVn is set in the timer clock in which TCNTn becomes zero and acts as a seventeenth bit that is only set; the overflow interrupt can extend the count in software. TCNTn may be written at any time. Compare units can time interrupts; generating waveforms in this mode costs too much CPU time.

WGMn3:0 = 4 (TOP = OCRnA) or 12 (TOP = ICRn). The counter clears when TCNTn reaches TOP, and OCFnA or ICFn (whichever register holds TOP) can interrupt each time. There is no double buffering: a TOP written below the current count makes the counter run to 0xFFFF and wrap before the next match. Fast PWM with OCRnA as TOP (WGMn3:0 = 15) avoids this, since OCRnA is then double buffered. With COMnA1:0 = 1, OCnA toggles on each match, up to fclk_I/O/2 with OCRnA = 0, once DDR_OCnA = 1. TOVn is set as the counter passes from MAX to 0x0000.

WGMn3:0 = 5, 6, 7 (TOP fixed at 0x00FF, 0x01FF, 0x03FF: 8, 9 or 10 bits), 14 (TOP = ICRn) or 15 (TOP = OCRnA). Single slope from BOTTOM to TOP, clearing in the next timer clock; non-inverting output clears OCnx on the match and sets it at BOTTOM, inverting does the reverse. Resolution runs from 2 bits (TOP = 0x0003) to 16 bits (TOP = MAX). TOVn is set at TOP, and OCFnA or ICFn is set in the same timer clock when that register is TOP. A new TOP must be at least every compare value or those matches never happen; with a fixed TOP, unused compare bits are masked to zero on write. ICRn is not double buffered, so lowering it while running fast can miss TOP and wrap through 0xFFFF; OCRnA is buffered and takes its new value at the next TOP, as TCNTn clears and TOVn sets. ICRn as TOP suits a fixed frequency and frees OCRnA for PWM; OCRnA as TOP is better when the frequency changes. OCRnx = BOTTOM gives a spike every TOP+1 clocks; OCRnx = TOP gives a steady level. With OCRnA as TOP (mode 15) and COMnA1:0 = 1, OCnA gives a 50 % square wave up to fclk_I/O/2.

WGMn3:0 = 1, 2, 3 (TOP fixed at 0x00FF, 0x01FF, 0x03FF), 10 (TOP = ICRn) or 11 (TOP = OCRnA). Dual slope, BOTTOM to TOP and back, holding TOP for one timer clock; non-inverting output clears OCnx on the match counting up and sets it on the match counting down. Resolution 2 to 16 bits. TOVn is set at BOTTOM; OCFnA or ICFn is set at TOP, when the compare registers take their buffered values. A new TOP must be at least every compare value. Because the update happens at TOP, changing TOP while running makes the falling slope follow the old TOP and the rising slope the new one, so a period can come out asymmetric; phase and frequency correct mode is recommended when TOP changes at run time, and with a static TOP the two modes behave practically the same. Non-inverted, OCRnx = BOTTOM holds the output low and OCRnx = TOP holds it high. With OCRnA as TOP (mode 11) and COMnA1:0 = 1, OCnA toggles at 50 % duty.

operation.topic: Timer/Counter1 phase and frequency correct PWM mode
operation.text: WGMn3:0 = 8 (TOP = ICRn) or 9 (TOP = OCRnA). Dual slope like phase correct PWM, but the compare registers take their buffered values at BOTTOM, so both slopes of every period are equal and the output stays symmetric and frequency correct even when TOP changes. Resolution 2 to 16 bits. TOVn is set at BOTTOM with the update; OCFnA or ICFn is set when the count reaches TOP. A new TOP must be at least every compare value. ICRn as TOP suits a fixed frequency and frees OCRnA; OCRnA as TOP is better when the frequency changes. Non-inverted, OCRnx = BOTTOM holds the output low and OCRnx = TOP sets it high. With OCRnA as TOP (mode 9) and COMnA1:0 = 1, OCnA toggles at 50 % duty.

clkTn is a clock enable on clkI/O. OCFnx is set one timer clock after TCNTn equals OCRnx. In CTC and fast PWM the count goes TOP to BOTTOM; in the two dual-slope PWM modes it turns at TOP and counts down. TOVn (fast PWM) and ICFn (when ICRn is TOP) are set as the count leaves TOP, and in modes that update at TOP the compare register takes its new value then; in phase and frequency correct mode the same happens at BOTTOM. With the prescaler these events follow the prescaled clock.

An 8-bit timer/counter with two compare outputs (OC2A, OC2B), clear-on-compare, glitch-free phase correct PWM, a frequency generator, a 10-bit prescaler and overflow and compare interrupts (TOV2, OCF2A, OCF2B). It can run from a 32 kHz watch crystal on TOSC1/TOSC2 independently of the I/O clock. PRTIM2 in PRR0 must be zero for it to run. TCNT2, OCR2A and OCR2B are 8-bit; flags are in TIFR2 and masks in TIMSK2.

By default clkT2 is the I/O clock clkI/O. Writing AS2 in ASSR to one takes the clock from the Timer/Counter oscillator on TOSC1 and TOSC2 instead, under control of the asynchronous status register ASSR. CS22:0 select the prescaled clock; CS22:0 = 0 stops the timer, though TCNT2 stays readable and writable, and a CPU write wins over a clear or count.

WGM21:0 in TCCR2A and WGM22 in TCCR2B set the count sequence; TOV2 is set as the mode defines. TCNT2 is compared with OCR2A and OCR2B continuously; a match sets OCF2A or OCF2B on the next timer clock and can interrupt, and the flag clears when the interrupt runs or when one is written to it. OCR2x is double buffered in the PWM modes, updated at TOP or BOTTOM; in Normal and CTC it is written directly. FOC2x forces a match in non-PWM modes without setting the flag or clearing the timer. A CPU write to TCNT2 blocks any match in the next timer clock, even stopped; writing TCNT2 equal to OCR2x loses that match, and BOTTOM should not be written while counting down. Set OC2x up before making its pin an output; OC2x keeps its value across mode changes. COM2x1:0 are not double buffered and act at once.

With either COM2x1:0 bit set, OC2x drives its pin in place of the port value once DDR makes the pin an output, whatever the waveform mode. Some COM2x1:0 settings are reserved in some modes. A new COM2x1:0 acts at the next match, or at once through FOC2x in non-PWM modes.

Normal (WGM22:0 = 0): counts up through 0xFF to 0x00 with no clear; TOV2 is set as TCNT2 becomes zero and acts as a ninth bit; TCNT2 may be written at any time; making waveforms with the compare unit in this mode costs too much CPU time. CTC (WGM22:0 = 2): the counter clears when TCNT2 matches OCR2A, which sets TOP. Without double buffering, a TOP written below the current count makes the counter run to 0xFF and wrap first. With COM2A1:0 = 1, OC2A toggles on each match, up to fclk_I/O/2 with OCR2A = 0. TOV2 is set as the count passes from MAX to 0x00.

WGM22:0 = 3 (TOP = 0xFF) or 7 (TOP = OCR2A). Single slope from BOTTOM to TOP, clearing in the next timer clock, giving up to twice the frequency of phase correct PWM. Non-inverting output (COM2x1:0 = 2) clears OC2x on the match and sets it at BOTTOM; inverting (3) is the reverse. TOV2 is set at TOP. OCR2A = BOTTOM gives a narrow spike every MAX+1 timer clocks; OCR2A = MAX a steady level set by COM2A1:0. Toggling OC2x on each match (COM2x1:0 = 1) gives a 50 % square wave of up to fclk_I/O/2 with OCR2A = 0, with double-buffered compare values.

WGM22:0 = 1 (TOP = 0xFF) or 5 (TOP = OCR2A). Dual slope, BOTTOM to TOP and back, holding TOP for one timer clock; non-inverting output clears OC2x on the up-count match and sets it on the down-count match. TOV2 is set at BOTTOM. Non-inverted, OCR2A = BOTTOM holds the output low and OCR2A = MAX holds it high. As with Timer/Counter0, OC2x can change at the start of a period without a match, to keep symmetry about BOTTOM, when OCR2A moves away from MAX or when the count starts above OCR2A.

In synchronous mode clkT2 is a clock enable on clkI/O; in asynchronous mode the Timer/Counter oscillator clock takes the place of clkI/O. TOV2 is set as the count passes from MAX to BOTTOM (all modes but phase correct PWM); OCF2A is set one timer clock after TCNT2 equals OCR2A (all modes but CTC); in CTC, OCF2A is set and TCNT2 cleared as the count leaves TOP.

Switching between asynchronous and synchronous clocking can corrupt TCNT2, OCR2x and TCCR2x. Safe order: disable the Timer/Counter2 interrupts (OCIE2x, TOIE2); set AS2 as wanted; write TCNT2, OCR2x and TCCR2x; when going asynchronous, wait until TCN2UB, OCR2xUB and TCR2xUB clear; clear the Timer/Counter2 interrupt flags; re-enable interrupts if needed. In asynchronous mode the CPU clock must exceed four times the 32 kHz oscillator's frequency.

A write to TCNT2, OCR2x or TCCR2x goes to a temporary register of its own and is latched after two rising edges on TOSC1; no new value should be written to the same register until the transfer is done, which the update-busy flags in ASSR show. Writes to different registers do not disturb each other.

Before entering Power-save or ADC Noise Reduction with Timer/Counter2 as the wake-up source, wait until any register just written has updated; otherwise the part sleeps before the change takes effect, and since compare is disabled while OCR2x or TCNT2 is being written, a sleep entered before OCR2xUB clears can miss the compare interrupt and never wake. After a Timer/Counter2 wake-up the interrupt logic needs one TOSC1 cycle to reset, so re-entering sleep sooner fails to wake; to make sure a cycle has passed, write TCCR2x, TCNT2 or OCR2x, wait for its busy flag to clear, then sleep.

In asynchronous mode the 32.768 kHz oscillator runs in every mode except Power-down and Standby. After power-up, or on leaving Power-down or Standby, it may take up to one second to settle; wait at least one second before using Timer/Counter2. Leaving Power-down or Standby, treat every Timer/Counter2 register as corrupted, whether a crystal or an external clock on TOSC1 is used.

From Power-save or ADC Noise Reduction with an asynchronous clock, wake-up starts on the timer clock after the interrupt condition, so the count has moved on by one or more before the CPU can read it; the MCU then halts four cycles, runs the interrupt and continues after SLEEP. TCNT2 is read through a register synchronised on each rising TOSC1 edge, so just after a wake-up from Power-save it shows the value from before sleep until the next rising edge, whose phase is unpredictable. To read it reliably: write any value to OCR2x or TCCR2x, wait for that busy flag to clear, then read TCNT2. Interrupt flag synchronisation takes three CPU cycles plus one timer cycle. The compare pin changes on the timer clock, not synchronised to the CPU clock.

The prescaler input clkT2S is the I/O clock by default. With AS2 set, it comes from TOSC1, and TOSC1 and TOSC2 are disconnected from Port C so a crystal can be connected across them; the oscillator is optimised for a 32.768 kHz crystal, which lets Timer/Counter2 serve as a real-time counter. Setting EXCLK in ASSR accepts a 32 kHz external clock instead. Selections are stop, clkT2S, clkT2S/8, /32, /64, /128, /256 and /1024. PSRASY in GTCCR resets the prescaler so its phase is known.

A full-duplex three-wire synchronous serial port for the part's peripherals or other AVRs: master or slave, LSB or MSB first, seven bit rates, an end-of-transmission interrupt flag, write collision protection, wake-up from Idle, and a double-speed (CK/2) master mode. A USART can also run as an SPI master. PRSPI in PRR0 must be zero for it to run.

The master starts a transfer by pulling the chosen slave's S̅S̅ low; the SPI master does not drive S̅S̅ itself, so software must. Writing a byte to SPDR starts the clock generator; eight bits shift out on MOSI while eight shift in on MISO, then the clock stops and SPIF is set, with an interrupt when SPIE in SPCR is set. The master writes the next byte to SPDR or raises S̅S̅ to end the packet. The last byte received stays in the buffer register.

While S̅S̅ is high the slave sleeps with MISO tri-stated; SPDR can be loaded but nothing shifts until S̅S̅ goes low. After each complete byte SPIF is set and the interrupt follows when enabled. The slave may load the next byte to send before reading what came in. SCK low and high periods must each be longer than two CPU clock cycles for the slave to sample the clock correctly.

Transmit is single buffered: a new byte cannot be written to SPDR until the shift is complete. Receive is double buffered: a received byte must be read before the next one has fully shifted in, or the first is lost.

To set up a master, make MOSI and SCK outputs and the rest inputs, then write SPCR with SPE, MSTR and the rate bits (SPR0 alone gives fck/16); to send, write SPDR and wait for SPIF in SPSR. To set up a slave, make MISO an output and set SPE; to receive, wait for SPIF and read SPDR.

As slave, S̅S̅ is always an input. Held low it activates the SPI and lets MISO drive if set as an output; driven high it makes every pin an input, the SPI ignores incoming data, and the send and receive logic reset at once, dropping any partial byte. This keeps the slave's bit count in step with the master packet by packet.

With MSTR set the direction of S̅S̅ is the user's choice. As an output it is an ordinary pin, typically driving a slave's S̅S̅. As an input it has to stay high; if something pulls it low the SPI takes it as another master selecting it, clears MSTR so it becomes a slave with MOSI and SCK as inputs, and sets SPIF, running the interrupt if enabled with the I-bit set. An interrupt-driven master that might see S̅S̅ pulled low should check MSTR in its handler and set it again if it was cleared.

CPOL and CPHA give four combinations of clock polarity and phase. Data shifts out on one SCK edge and is latched on the other, leaving time for the lines to settle. DORD = 0 sends the MSB first, DORD = 1 the LSB first.

Two USARTs, USART0 and USART1, each with its own I/O registers. Each is full duplex with separate receive and transmit registers, asynchronous or synchronous (master or slave clocked), with a high-resolution baud rate generator, frames of 5, 6, 7, 8 or 9 data bits and 1 or 2 stop bits, hardware odd or even parity generation and checking, overrun and framing error detection, noise filtering with false start bit detection and a digital low-pass filter, three interrupts (TX complete, TX data register empty, RX complete), multi-processor communication mode and double-speed asynchronous mode. PRUSART0 in PRR0 and PRUSART1 in PRR1 must be zero for the USARTs to run.

Three parts share the control registers: a clock generator (baud rate generator and synchronisation for an external clock in synchronous slave mode), a transmitter (one write buffer, shift register, parity generator and frame control; the buffer allows back-to-back frames) and a receiver (clock and data recovery for asynchronous reception, parity checker, shift register, and UDRn as a receive buffer two entries deep). The receiver handles the same frame formats and detects frame errors, overruns and parity errors. XCKn is used only in synchronous mode.

Four clock modes: asynchronous at normal or double speed, and synchronous as master or as slave. UMSELn in UCSRnC chooses asynchronous or synchronous; U2Xn in UCSRnA sets double speed (asynchronous only). In synchronous mode (UMSELn = 1) the XCKn DDR bit chooses an internal clock (master, output) or an external one (slave, input).

UBRRn and a down-counter running at fOSC form the baud rate generator: the counter reloads from UBRRn each time it reaches zero or UBRRnL is written, and gives a clock pulse at each zero, fOSC/(UBRRn+1). The transmitter divides this by 2, 8 or 16 according to mode; the receiver's recovery units use it directly, with a state machine of 2, 8 or 16 states set by UMSELn, U2Xn and DDR_XCKn. UBRRn (UBRRnH and UBRRnL) holds 0 to 4095.

U2Xn = 1 halves the asynchronous divisor from 16 to 8 and so doubles the rate. The receiver then takes 8 samples per bit in place of 16 for data and clock recovery, so the baud setting and system clock must be more accurate; the transmitter is unaffected. Keep U2Xn zero in synchronous mode.

In synchronous slave mode XCKn is sampled by a synchroniser and passed through an edge detector, which adds two CPU clocks of delay and limits the external clock to fOSC/4. Leave some margin, since fOSC moves with the stability of the system clock.

With UMSELn = 1, XCKn is the clock input (slave) or output (master). Received data on RxDn is sampled on the opposite XCKn edge from the one on which TxDn changes. UCPOLn = 0: data changes on the rising edge and is sampled on the falling edge. UCPOLn = 1: changes on falling, sampled on rising.

A frame is one start bit (always low), 5 to 9 data bits LSB first, an optional even or odd parity bit after the data, and one or two stop bits (high); 30 combinations in all. A frame can follow the last stop bit directly, or the line idles high. UCSZn2:0 set the data bits, UPMn1:0 the parity and USBSn the stop bits; receiver and transmitter share the setting, and changing it corrupts any transfer in progress. The receiver ignores a second stop bit, so a frame error is flagged only when the first stop bit reads zero.

Before use, set the baud rate and frame format and enable the transmitter and/or receiver; for interrupt-driven use, clear the global interrupt flag and disable the USART interrupts while doing so. Before changing the baud rate or frame format, make sure no transfer is in progress: TXCn shows the transmitter has finished (clear it before each write to UDRn if it is used this way) and RXCn shows unread data. An example setting is UBRRnH:UBRRnL from the baud parameter, RXENn and TXENn in UCSRnB, and USBSn with UCSZn = 3 for 8 data bits and 2 stop bits.

TXENn in UCSRnB enables the transmitter, which then owns TxDn as its serial output; in synchronous mode XCKn is overridden as the transmit clock. Writing UDRn loads the transmit buffer; the byte moves to the shift register when it is idle or right after the previous frame's last stop bit, and is sent at the rate set by the baud register, U2Xn or XCKn. With fewer than eight data bits the unused high bits written to UDRn are ignored. A simple sender waits for UDREn and then writes UDRn.

With 9-bit characters (UCSZn = 7) the ninth bit goes into TXB8n in UCSRnB before the low byte is written to UDRn. The ninth bit can mark an address frame in multi-processor mode or carry other protocol information.

UDREn is set while the transmit buffer is empty and clear while it holds data not yet moved to the shift register; write it as zero when writing UCSRnA. With UDRIEn set, the data register empty interrupt runs as long as UDREn is set, so its handler must write UDRn or disable the interrupt, or it runs again at once. TXCn is set when the whole frame has left the shift register and the buffer is empty; it clears when the transmit complete interrupt (TXCIEn) runs or when one is written to it. TXCn suits half-duplex buses such as RS-485, where the sender must release the bus right after the last bit.

With UPMn1 = 1 the parity generator adds the parity bit after the final data bit, ahead of the stop bits. Clearing TXENn takes effect only after the frames in the shift register and buffer have gone; the transmitter then releases TxDn.

RXENn in UCSRnB enables the receiver, which then owns RxDn as its serial input; in synchronous mode XCKn is the transfer clock. On a valid start bit each following bit is sampled at the baud rate or on XCKn and shifted in until the first stop bit; a second stop bit is ignored. The complete frame then moves to the receive buffer, read through UDRn. With fewer than eight data bits the unused high bits read as zero. A simple receiver waits for RXCn and then reads UDRn.

With 9-bit characters, read RXB8n in UCSRnB before the low byte in UDRn. The same applies to the status flags FEn, DORn and UPEn: read UCSRnA first, then UDRn, because reading UDRn advances the receive FIFO and changes the ninth bit and status bits held with each entry. Reading all the registers before processing frees the buffer location as early as possible.

RXCn is one while the receive buffer holds unread data and zero when it is empty; disabling the receiver flushes the buffer and clears RXCn. With RXCIEn set the receive complete interrupt runs as long as RXCn is set, so its handler must read UDRn or it runs again at once.

The error flags in UCSRnA (FEn for a framing fault, DORn for overrun, UPEn for parity) are stored in the receive buffer with the frame they describe, so UCSRnA must be read before UDRn. Software cannot change them by writing, but should write them as zero when writing UCSRnA. None of them raises an interrupt. FEn is one when the next frame waiting in the buffer had a zero first stop bit, and is useful for spotting loss of sync, break conditions and protocol events; USBSn does not affect it. DORn is set when the two-character buffer is full, a third character waits in the shift register and a new start bit arrives; it means one or more frames were lost between the last frame read and the next, and it clears when a received frame moves into the buffer. UPEn is set when the next frame in the buffer had a parity error while checking was on (UPMn1 = 1), stays valid until UDRn is read, and always reads zero with parity checking off.

Active when UPMn1 is set; UPMn0 chooses odd or even. It computes the parity of each incoming frame's data bits, compares it with the received parity bit, and stores the result with the frame for UPEn.

Unlike the transmitter, the receiver stops at once when RXENn is cleared: a frame in progress is lost, the FIFO is flushed and RxDn returns to normal port use. To empty the buffer during operation, for example after an error, read UDRn until RXCn clears.

Clock recovery locks the internal baud clock to each incoming frame at RxDn; data recovery samples and low-pass filters every bit for noise immunity. The working range depends on the baud clock accuracy, the incoming rate and the frame length.

Sampling runs at 16 times the baud rate in normal mode and 8 times in double-speed mode, which leaves more timing uncertainty. A high-to-low transition on idle RxDn starts start-bit detection; counting the first low sample as 1, samples 8, 9 and 10 (normal) or 4, 5 and 6 (double speed) decide it by majority. If two or more are high the edge is rejected as a spike and the receiver waits for the next falling edge; otherwise clock recovery synchronises and data recovery begins. This repeats for every start bit.

A state machine with 16 states per bit (normal) or 8 (double speed) samples each data and parity bit; the three centre samples decide the bit by majority vote, which acts as a low-pass filter on RxDn. This continues to the first stop bit, the only one used. A stop bit voted zero sets FEn. The next start bit may begin right after the last voting sample of the stop bit in normal mode; in double-speed mode it must come a little later. This early start detection affects the operating range.

If the incoming bit rate is too far from the receiver's own baud rate, the receiver cannot hold frames in step with the start bit. Normal speed tolerates more baud rate error than double speed. The recommended receiver error assumes the receiver and transmitter share the maximum total error equally. The receiver's error has two sources: system clock drift over supply and temperature, rarely an issue with a crystal but possibly over 2 % with a resonator; and the baud rate generator's inability to divide the clock exactly, where a UBRR value with acceptably low error should be chosen.

Setting MPCMn in UCSRnA makes the receiver discard frames that carry no address, so on a shared bus each MCU handles fewer frames. The transmitter is unaffected but is used differently. With 5 to 8 data bits the first stop bit marks the frame type; with 9 data bits the ninth bit (RXB8n) does. A one marks an address frame, a zero a data frame. Slaves decode the address frame; the one addressed takes the following data frames, the rest ignore them until the next address frame.

The master can use 9-bit frames (UCSZn = 7) with TXB8n = 1 for an address and 0 for data; the slaves then also use 9-bit frames. Sequence: all slaves set MPCMn; the master sends an address frame, which every slave receives with RXCn set as usual; each slave reads UDRn and, if selected, clears MPCMn, otherwise keeps it and waits; the addressed slave takes every data frame until the next address frame while the others ignore them; after its last data frame it sets MPCMn again and waits. 5- to 8-bit frames work but are awkward, since the receiver must switch between n and n+1 bit frames, which hampers full duplex as both directions share the size setting; the transmitter then needs two stop bits (USBSn = 1). Do not set or clear MPCMn with SBI or CBI: it shares its I/O location with TXCn, which they can clear by accident.

For common crystal and resonator frequencies, UBRRn settings exist that give the usual asynchronous baud rates. Settings within 0.5 % of the target are the preferred ones. Larger errors still work, but the receiver loses noise margin, more so with long frames.

Each USART can act as an SPI master: full duplex three-wire, all four SPI modes, LSB or MSB first, double-buffered queued operation, the high-resolution baud rate generator, up to fXCKmax = fCK/2, and flexible interrupts. Setting both UMSELn1:0 bits selects it. The SPI master logic then drives the USART's shift registers, buffers and baud rate generator directly; the parity generator and checker, clock and data recovery and the RX and TX control logic are off, replaced by one SPI transfer control. Pin control and interrupt generation work as in USART mode. The register addresses are the same, though some control bits change meaning.

Only an internal clock (master) is supported, so DDR_XCKn must be one, preferably set before TXENn and RXENn. The clock generator works as in synchronous master mode and the same equation gives UBRRn.
UCPHAn and UCPOLn set the four combinations of XCKn phase and polarity; data shifts out and is latched on opposite edges. Changing either bit corrupts any transfer in progress in both directions.

A frame is eight data bits, MSB first or LSB first as UDORDn in UCSRnC sets for both directions; changing it corrupts a transfer in progress. Frames may follow back to back or the line idles high. Writing two bytes to UDRn sends 16 bits, and the transmit complete interrupt marks the end of both.

Set the baud rate, make XCKn an output for master mode, set the frame format, and enable the transmitter and receiver; only the transmitter can work alone. For interrupt-driven use, keep interrupts globally disabled during set-up. For the XCKn output to start at once, UBRRn must be zero when the transmitter is enabled, and the real UBRRn value is written after enabling the transmitter but before the first transfer; right after reset UBRRn is already zero. Before changing baud rate, data mode or frame format, make sure no transfer is running, using TXCn (cleared before each UDRn write if used so) and RXCn. A typical order: UBRRn = 0; set the XCKn DDR bit; UCSRnC with UMSELn1, UMSELn0 and the mode bits (SPI mode 0 in the example); RXENn and TXENn in UCSRnB; then UBRRn.

The transmitter must be enabled (TXENn), and it then owns TxDn; enabling the receiver (RXENn) is optional and gives it RxDn. XCKn is the transfer clock in both cases. Every transfer, send or receive, starts with a write to UDRn, because the transmitter drives the clock; the byte moves from the buffer to the shift register when that is ready for a new frame.

UDRn must be read once for every byte sent to keep the receive buffer in step with the transfers. On overflow the newest byte is the one lost, as in normal USART mode: send four bytes without reading and byte 3 is lost, not byte 1. A simple transfer waits for UDREn, writes UDRn, waits for RXCn and reads UDRn. RXCn, TXCn and UDREn and their interrupts behave as in normal USART mode; the error flags FE, DOR and PE are unused and read zero. Disabling the transmitter or receiver works as in normal mode.

MSPIM matches the SPI's master timing, and UCPOLn, UCPHAn and UDORDn act like CPOL, CPHA and DORD. It differs in that it is master only, its transmitter is double buffered where the SPI has no buffer, its receiver has an extra buffer level, it has no write collision bit WCOL and no SPI2X bit (UBRRn gives the same effect), its interrupt timing is not compatible, and its pin control differs.

A two-line bus interface, SCL for clock and SDA for data, working as master or slave and as transmitter or receiver. It has a 7-bit address space for up to 128 slave addresses, multi-master arbitration, transfer rates up to 400 kHz, slew-rate limited output drivers, noise suppression that rejects spikes on the bus lines, a slave address set entirely by software, with general call support, and address recognition that wakes the AVR from sleep. Each bus line needs one pull-up resistor; every device has its own address and the protocol settles bus contention. PRTWI in PRR0 must be zero for the TWI to run.

Both lines are pulled to the positive supply by resistors, and the drivers of every TWI-compliant device are open-drain or open-collector, forming a wired-AND: a line is low when any device drives a zero and high when all release it. Every AVR on the bus must be powered for the bus to work. The number of devices is limited only by the 400 pF bus capacitance limit and the 7-bit address space. Separate electrical specifications cover bus speeds below 100 kHz and up to 400 kHz.

Each data bit comes with a clock pulse, and SDA must be stable while SCL is high, except for START and STOP. The master issues START to begin a transfer and STOP to end it; between them the bus is busy and other masters should not take it. A START issued before the STOP is a REPEATED START, used to begin a new transfer without releasing the bus, which then stays busy until the next STOP. START and STOP are signalled by SDA changing while SCL is high.

An address packet is 9 bits: 7 address bits sent MSB first, a READ/WRITE bit (one for read) and an acknowledge bit. An addressed slave acknowledges by holding SDA low during clock nine; a busy or unable slave leaves SDA high, and the master can then send STOP or REPEATED START. The packets are called SLA+R and SLA+W. Addresses are free to choose, except that 0000 000 is the general call and 1111 xxx are reserved. On a general call followed by a write bit, every slave set to acknowledge it pulls SDA low and receives the data that follows; a general call with a read bit makes no sense, since slaves would contend.

A data packet is 9 bits: one byte, MSB first, and an acknowledge bit. The master drives the clock and START and STOP; the receiver acknowledges by pulling SDA low in the ninth cycle, and leaves it high (NACK) after the last byte or when it can take no more. A transmission is START, then SLA+R/W, then at least one data packet, then STOP; START followed directly by STOP is illegal. A slave may stretch the SCL low period to slow the master or gain processing time between bytes; the high period stays the master's.

operation.topic: TWI multi-master arbitration and clock synchronisation
operation.text: When masters start together, one must win (arbitration) without the slaves noticing or data being corrupted, and differing SCL frequencies must be brought into lockstep. The wired-AND solves both: the combined SCL high period equals the shortest master high period and the low period the longest master low period, every master timing from the combined line's edges. Each master reads SDA after driving it; one that drives high while another drives low has lost, must release SDA at once and switch to slave mode to see if it is being addressed, though it may keep clocking to the end of the current packet. Arbitration can take many bits and, with several masters addressing the same slave, continue into the data. It is not allowed between a REPEATED START and a data bit, a STOP and a data bit, or a REPEATED START and a STOP; software must prevent these, so in multi-master systems every transfer must have the same mix of SLA+R/W and data packets, or the outcome is undefined.

The module has SCL and SDA pin stages, a bit rate generator, a bus interface unit, an address match unit and a control unit; TWBR, TWSR, TWDR, TWAR and TWCR are reached over the data bus. The output drivers have slew-rate limiting to meet the TWI specification and the inputs suppress spikes shorter than 50 ns. The pins' internal pull-ups, turned on by their PORT bits, can in some systems replace external pull-ups.

In master mode TWBR and the prescaler bits in TWSR set the SCL period. Slave operation does not depend on them, but the slave's CPU clock must be at least 16 times the SCL frequency. Slaves may stretch SCL low and so lower the average bus clock. Choose the pull-up resistors from the SCL frequency and the bus capacitance.

operation.topic: TWI bus interface and address match
operation.text: The bus interface holds TWDR (the address or data byte to send or just received), an internal (N)ACK register (set by TWCR when receiving, reported in TWSR when transmitting), a START/STOP controller and arbitration detection. START and STOP are detected even in sleep, so the MCU can wake when a master addresses it. When the TWI is master, arbitration detection watches the bus and reports a lost arbitration to the control unit. The address match unit compares received addresses with the 7-bit address in TWAR, and with the general call address when TWGCE is set, also during sleep; whether the TWI acknowledges depends on TWCR.

When a bus event needs the application, TWINT is set and TWSR receives a status code in the next clock; at other times TWSR holds a code meaning no relevant information. While TWINT is set SCL is held low, so the application can finish before the transfer continues. TWINT is set after the TWI has sent START or REPEATED START, sent SLA+R/W, sent an address byte, lost arbitration, recognised its own address or a general call addressed to it, received a data byte, received STOP or REPEATED START while still addressed as slave, and on a bus error from an illegal START or STOP.

The TWI is byte oriented and interrupt driven: an interrupt follows every bus event, so the CPU is free during a byte. TWIE with the global interrupt enable decides whether TWINT raises an interrupt; with TWIE clear the application polls TWINT. With TWINT set, TWSR shows the bus state and the application sets the next step through TWCR and TWDR. Writing a one to TWINT clears it, and the TWI does nothing while TWINT is set; the operation begins as soon as it is cleared. So: load every TWI register for the next bus cycle (TWDR with the byte to send, for instance), then write TWCR with TWINT set. A master sending one byte writes TWCR to send START; checks TWSR for the START code, loads SLA+W into TWDR and writes TWCR; checks for SLA+W sent with ACK, loads the data and writes TWCR; checks for data sent with ACK; then writes TWCR to send STOP. TWINT is not set after a STOP has gone. Status is checked with the prescaler bits masked (TWSR & 0xF8).

Four modes: MT (master transmitter), MR (master receiver), ST (slave transmitter) and SR (slave receiver); an application can use several, for example MT to write a TWI EEPROM and MR to read it back. At each point where TWINT is set, TWSR holds a status code (prescaler bits masked to zero) and the transfer waits until software clears TWINT. Symbols: S START, Rs REPEATED START, R read bit (SDA high), W write bit (SDA low), A acknowledge (SDA low), A̅ not acknowledge (SDA high), Data an 8-bit byte, P STOP, SLA slave address.

A master mode is entered by sending START; the address packet that follows chooses MT (SLA+W) or MR (SLA+R). After START, TWINT sets with status 0x08; write SLA+W to TWDR and clear TWINT. After the address and acknowledge, the status is 0x18, 0x20 or 0x38. Then write each data byte to TWDR and clear TWINT; TWDR may be written only while TWINT is high, or the write is discarded and TWWC set. End with STOP, or with REPEATED START (status 0x10), which lets the master address the same or another slave, or switch between MT and MR, without releasing the bus.

A successful write to a slave receiver runs S, SLA, W, A (0x08 then 0x18), data, A (0x28), P. A NACK after the address gives 0x20, after a data byte 0x30. Arbitration lost in the address or a data byte gives 0x38; lost and then addressed as slave leads to 0x68, 0x78 or 0xB0 in slave mode. A REPEATED START gives 0x10 and can lead into MR by sending SLA+R.
