After START (0x08), write SLA+R to TWDR and clear TWINT. After the address and acknowledge the status is 0x38, 0x40 or 0x48. Each received byte is read from TWDR when TWINT is set. After the last byte the master receiver sends NACK to tell the slave transmitter, then ends with STOP or REPEATED START (0x10).

A successful read runs S, SLA, R, A (0x08 then 0x40), data, A (0x50) for each byte but the last, then data, A̅ (0x58), P. A NACK after the address gives 0x48. Arbitration lost gives 0x38; lost and addressed as slave leads to 0x68, 0x78 or 0xB0. A REPEATED START gives 0x10 and can lead into MT by sending SLA+W.

TWAR holds the device's own 7-bit slave address in its upper seven bits; setting its LSB (TWGCE) makes the TWI also answer the general call address 0x00. TWCR is set with TWEN and TWEA one and TWSTA and TWSTO zero. The TWI then waits for its own address (or the general call) and the direction bit: a write bit enters SR, a read bit ST. TWINT then sets with a valid status. SR is also entered when arbitration is lost as master (0x68, 0x78). Clearing TWEA during a transfer returns NACK after the next byte, signalling that no more can be taken; while TWEA is zero the TWI ignores its own address but keeps watching the bus, and setting TWEA resumes address recognition, so TWEA can isolate the TWI from the bus for a while.

In every sleep mode except Idle the TWI's clock is off. With TWEA set the TWI can still acknowledge its own address or the general call using the bus clock; the part then wakes, and the TWI holds SCL low through the wake-up until TWINT is cleared, after which transfers continue normally with the AVR clocks running. A long start-up time can therefore hold SCL low long enough to block other traffic. TWDR does not show the last byte on the bus after waking from these modes.

Own address and acknowledged bytes: S, SLA, W, A (0x60), data, A (0x80) per byte, ending with P or S (0xA0); a last byte answered with NACK gives 0x88. After losing arbitration as master and being addressed, the code is 0x68. The general call follows the same pattern with 0x70, 0x90, 0x98 and 0xA0, and 0x78 after lost arbitration.

TWAR and TWCR are set as for slave receiver. On its own address (or the general call) with a read bit the TWI enters ST and sets TWINT with a valid status; ST is also entered after lost arbitration (0xB0). If TWEA is cleared during a transfer, the TWI sends the last byte and enters 0xC0 or 0xC8 depending on whether the master answers NACK or ACK; it then switches to not-addressed slave mode and ignores the master, which reads all ones. 0xC8 means the master asked for more data after the slave had sent its last byte. While TWEA is zero the TWI ignores its own address but monitors the bus. Address wake-up from sleep works as in slave receiver mode, holding SCL low until TWINT is cleared, and TWDR does not show the last bus byte after waking.

Own address and data: S, SLA, R, A (0xA8), data, A (0xB8) per byte, then data, A̅ (0xC0), P or S. Arbitration lost and addressed as slave gives 0xB0. After the last byte with TWEA = 0, an ACK from the master gives 0xC8 and the master then reads all ones until P or S.

Two codes match no defined state. 0xF8: TWINT is not set, so no relevant information is available; it appears between states and when the TWI is idle. 0x00: a bus error, a START or STOP in an illegal place such as within an address byte, data byte or acknowledge bit; TWINT is set. To recover, set TWSTO and clear TWINT by writing one; the TWI enters not-addressed slave mode and clears TWSTO without touching the other TWCR bits, and SDA and SCL are released with no STOP sent.

Some actions need more than one mode. Reading a serial EEPROM means starting the transfer, telling the EEPROM which location to read (MT), reading (MR) and finishing. The master must hold the bus throughout so the steps are atomic; otherwise in a multi-master system another master could move the EEPROM's pointer between setting it and reading. The change of direction is done with a REPEATED START between sending the address byte and receiving the data: START, SLA+W and ACK, the memory address and ACK, REPEATED START, SLA+R and ACK, then data, NACK and STOP.

When several masters start at once, the standard lets one proceed with no data lost. Masters doing identical transfers to the same slave never notice the contention. Masters that address one slave but differ in direction or data arbitrate in the R/W bit or the data; whoever sends a one while another sends a zero loses and, as software decides, goes to not-addressed slave mode or waits for a free bus and sends START again. Masters addressing different slaves arbitrate in the SLA bits; losers switch to slave mode and, if addressed by the winner, to SR or ST by the R/W bit, otherwise to not-addressed slave mode or wait and retry. Lost in SLA or data: 0x38, or 0x68/0x78 when addressed with a write and 0xB0 with a read.

Compares the positive input AIN0 with the negative input AIN1 and sets its output ACO when AIN0 is higher. The output can trigger the Timer/Counter1 input capture and has its own interrupt, on a rising, falling or toggling output. A fixed bandgap reference can replace AIN0 (ACBG). PRADC in PRR0 must be zero to use the ADC input multiplexer.

Any of ADC7..0 can replace AIN1 as the negative input through the ADC multiplexer, so the ADC must be off: with ACME in ADCSRB set and ADEN in ADCSRA zero, MUX2..0 in ADMUX pick the pin. With ACME clear or ADEN set, AIN1 is the negative input.

ACD = 1 switches the comparator's power off, saving current in Active and Idle; clear ACIE before changing ACD, or the change can raise an interrupt. ACBG = 1 puts the bandgap reference on the positive input in place of AIN0; the reference needs time to settle, and an unsettled first result may be wrong. ACO is the comparator output after synchronisation, which delays it by 1 to 2 clock cycles. ACI is set when an output event matches the mode chosen by ACIS1:0, and the interrupt runs when both ACIE and the global I-bit are one.

A 10-bit successive approximation ADC with 0.5 LSB integral non-linearity, ±2 LSB absolute accuracy, 13 to 260 µs conversion time and up to 15 kSPS at full resolution. Inputs: eight single-ended channels on Port A, referred to 0 V (GND), and 16 differential combinations, with input range 0 to VCC single-ended and 2.7 V to VCC differential. Two differential pairs (ADC1, ADC0 and ADC3, ADC2) have a programmable gain stage of 0 dB (1×), 20 dB (10×) or 46 dB (200×); seven differential channels share ADC1 as negative input with any other ADC input as positive. Expect 8-bit resolution at 1× or 10× gain and 6-bit at 200×. Also: optional left-adjusted result, 2.56 V or 1.1 V internal reference, free running or single conversion, auto triggering from interrupt sources, a conversion complete interrupt and a sleep-mode noise canceler. A sample and hold keeps the input constant during conversion. The differential channels are not tested on the PDIP package and are guaranteed only in the TQFP, QFN-type (VQFN/QFN/MLF), DRQFN and VFBGA packages.

The ADC has its own analog supply pin AVCC, which must stay within ±0.3 V of VCC. On-chip references are nominally 1.1 V, 2.56 V or AVCC, and the reference can be decoupled with a capacitor at AREF for lower noise. The 1.1 V reference is not for use with 10× or 200× gain, and below VCC = 2.1 V it is not for single-ended channels either.

The result runs from GND (code 0) to the AREF voltage minus 1 LSB. REFSn in ADMUX can connect AVCC or the internal 2.56 V reference to AREF, where an external capacitor can then decouple it. MUX bits in ADMUX choose the channel and the differential gain: any ADC pin, GND or the fixed bandgap reference can be a single-ended input, and some ADC pins can be the positive and negative inputs of the gain amplifier, which is bypassed for single-ended channels. ADEN in ADCSRA enables the ADC; reference and channel choices take effect only once it is set. With ADEN clear the ADC draws no power, so it should be turned off before the power-saving sleep modes.

The 10-bit result sits in ADCH and ADCL, right adjusted by default or left adjusted with ADLAR in ADMUX. Left adjusted, reading ADCH alone gives 8 bits. Otherwise read ADCL first, then ADCH: reading ADCL locks the data registers until ADCH is read, and a conversion finishing in between is lost, though its interrupt still fires.

Writing one to ADSC starts a single conversion; ADSC reads one until it ends and is then cleared by hardware. A channel change during a conversion waits until it finishes. With ADATE in ADCSRA set, the source chosen by ADTS in ADCSRB starts conversions on its rising edge and resets the ADC prescaler, giving conversions at fixed intervals. If the trigger is still high when a conversion ends, no new one starts, and an edge during a conversion is ignored. The trigger's interrupt flag is set even with its interrupt disabled, so conversions can be triggered without interrupts, but that flag must be cleared before the next event can trigger again. Using ADIF itself as the trigger gives free running mode, where each conversion starts as the last ends, whether or not ADIF is cleared; the first is started with ADSC. With auto triggering on, ADSC can still start a single conversion, and it reads one during any conversion.

For full 10-bit resolution the converter needs a 50 kHz to 200 kHz clock; for less resolution it can run faster for a higher sample rate. A 7-bit prescaler (ADPS in ADCSRA, CK/2 to CK/128) derives this from any CPU clock above 100 kHz; it runs while ADEN is set and is held reset while ADEN is low. A single-ended conversion started by ADSC begins on the next rising ADC clock edge. A normal conversion takes 13 ADC clocks; the first after enabling takes 25, to initialise the analog circuits. Sample and hold happens 1.5 ADC clocks into a normal conversion and 13.5 into a first one. At the end the result is written and ADIF set (and ADSC cleared in single conversion mode); setting ADSC again starts the next on the first rising ADC clock edge. With auto triggering the prescaler resets on the trigger, giving a fixed delay: sample and hold comes 2 ADC clocks after the trigger's rising edge, plus three CPU clocks of synchronisation. Differential conversions auto-triggered from a source other than conversion complete need 25 ADC clocks each, because the ADC is disabled and re-enabled after every one. In free running mode a new conversion starts at once while ADSC stays high. The bandgap needs time to settle when used as the ADC input, and the first value read may be wrong.

Differential channels should not be used with AREF below 2 V. Differential conversions are synchronised to CKADC2, half the ADC clock, so that sample and hold falls at a fixed phase: a user-started conversion (every single conversion and the first free running one) takes 13 ADC clocks from the next prescaled clock if CKADC2 is low and 14 if it is high, and every automatically started free running conversion takes 14. The gain stage is optimised for 4 kHz bandwidth at every gain; higher frequencies may be amplified non-linearly, so filter inputs with faster content. The ADC clock is independent of that bandwidth: a 6 µs ADC clock period samples a channel at 12 kSPS whatever its bandwidth. With auto triggering the prescaler reset leaves the gain stage without the stable clock it needs, so that conversion is invalid; switch the ADC off and on (ADEN 0 then 1) between conversions so each is an extended, valid one.

MUXn and REFS1:0 pass through a temporary register so a change lands at a safe point: the selection follows the register until a conversion starts, is locked during it for enough sampling time, and follows again from the last ADC clock before completion (when ADIF sets). The conversion starts on the rising ADC clock after ADSC is written, so do not write ADMUX until one ADC clock after ADSC. With ADATE and ADEN both set, a trigger can come at any time, and a change then may or may not apply to the next conversion. ADMUX is safe to change when ADATE or ADEN is clear, during a conversion at least one ADC clock after the trigger, or after a conversion before the trigger's interrupt flag is cleared; the new setting then applies to the next conversion. After selecting a new differential channel the gain stage may take up to 125 µs to settle, so do not start conversions within 125 µs or discard their results; the same applies to the first differential conversion after a reference change.

In single conversion mode select the channel before starting; it may change one ADC clock after ADSC is written, but waiting for the conversion to end is simplest. In free running mode select the channel before the first conversion; changing it one ADC clock after ADSC, or after the first conversion ends, affects the conversion after next, since the next has already started on the old channel. The first result after switching to a differential gain channel may be inaccurate while the automatic offset cancellation settles and should preferably be discarded.

VREF sets the conversion range; single-ended inputs above VREF give codes near 0x3FF. VREF can be AVCC (through a passive switch), the internal 2.56 V reference (from the bandgap VBG through an internal amplifier) or the AREF pin. AREF connects directly to the ADC, so a capacitor from AREF to ground improves noise immunity, and VREF can be measured there with a high-impedance voltmeter. VREF is a high-impedance source and should carry only a capacitive load. With a fixed voltage on AREF the other reference options cannot be used, since they would be shorted to it; with nothing on AREF, AVCC and 2.56 V can be switched. Discard the first result after a reference change. With differential channels the reference must stay at least the specified margin below AVCC.

Conversions can run in ADC Noise Reduction or Idle sleep to cut noise from the CPU core and I/O. Procedure: with the ADC enabled and idle, single conversion mode selected and the conversion complete interrupt enabled, enter ADC Noise Reduction (or Idle); the conversion starts once the CPU halts. If no other interrupt comes first, the ADC interrupt wakes the CPU and runs; if another interrupt wakes it first, that one runs and the ADC interrupt follows when the conversion ends. The CPU stays active until the next SLEEP. The ADC is not turned off automatically in other sleep modes; clear ADEN before entering them to avoid excess current. If it is left on and differential conversions are wanted, switch it off and on after waking to get an extended, valid conversion.

A source on ADCn sees that pin's capacitance and leakage whether or not the channel is selected. When selected, it must charge the sample-and-hold capacitor (14 pF, returned to VCC/2) through the series input resistance (1 to 100 kΩ). The ADC is optimised for sources of about 10 kΩ or less, for which sampling time is negligible; a higher impedance needs longer to charge the capacitor, by a widely varying amount, so low-impedance sources and slowly changing signals are recommended. For differential gain channels the input differs, and the source impedance should stay below a few hundred kΩ. Neither kind of channel should carry components above the Nyquist frequency (fADC/2); filter them out first.

Keep analog signal paths short, run analog tracks over the analog ground plane and well away from fast digital tracks. Feed AVCC from the digital VCC through an LC network. Use the ADC noise canceler to reduce noise from the CPU. Port A pins used as digital outputs must not switch during a conversion.

The gain stage's built-in offset cancellation nulls most of the differential offset. The residue can be measured by selecting the same channel as both differential inputs and subtracted in software, bringing the offset on any channel below one LSB.

An n-bit single-ended ADC divides GND to VREF linearly into 2^n steps (LSBs), with codes 0 to 2^n − 1. Offset: how far the first transition (0x000 to 0x001) lies from its ideal point at 0.5 LSB. Gain error: after removing offset, how far the last transition (0x3FE to 0x3FF) lies from its ideal point 1.5 LSB below full scale. Integral non-linearity (INL): after removing offset and gain error, the largest deviation of any transition from its ideal place. Differential non-linearity (DNL): the largest deviation of any code width (between adjacent transitions) from the ideal 1 LSB. Quantization error: the 1 LSB band of inputs that share one code, always ±0.5 LSB. Absolute accuracy: the largest deviation of any unadjusted transition from ideal, everything at once: quantization, non-linearity, gain error, offset and differential error.
Differential codes run from 0x200 at −VREF/GAIN through 0x000 at zero to 0x1FF at +VREF/GAIN, in two's complement; the MSB (ADC9 in ADCH) is a quick sign test.

An IEEE 1149.1 JTAG port serves three uses: boundary-scan testing of the board, writing Flash, EEPROM, fuses and lock bits, and on-chip debugging. Through it a debugger reaches every peripheral, the internal and external RAM, the register file, the program counter, and the EEPROM and Flash. Debug break conditions include the AVR BREAK instruction, a change of program flow, single step, and program or data memory break points on one address or an address range. The on-chip debug instructions are private and given only to Atmel and chosen tool vendors.

A TAP controller, a state machine run by TCK and TMS, places either the 4-bit instruction register or one of the data registers between TDI and TDO. The ID register, bypass register and boundary-scan chain are for board test; the programming interface is a set of physical and virtual data registers; two further chains, internal and break-point, are used by the debugger alone.

Four pins form the TAP: TMS (mode select, steers the state machine), TCK (the clock all JTAG operation follows), TDI (serial data into the instruction or data register) and TDO (serial data out). The optional TRST reset signal is absent. With the JTAGEN fuse unprogrammed the four pins are ordinary port pins and the TAP controller is held reset; programmed, the TAP inputs get internal pull-ups and JTAG is live for boundary scan and programming. Parts leave the factory with JTAGEN programmed. The debugger also watches RESET to see external resets, and may drive it low to reset the system, which requires that only open-collector drivers sit on the reset line.

A 16-state machine; each transition follows the level on TMS at a rising TCK edge, and power-on reset leaves it in Test-Logic-Reset. Every shift register shifts least significant bit first. From Run-Test/Idle, TMS = 1, 1, 0, 0 reaches Shift-IR; the four instruction bits then enter from TDI on rising TCK with TMS low for the three low bits and high for the last, which also leaves the state; meanwhile TDO shifts out the captured IR value 0x01. TMS = 1, 1, 0 returns to Run-Test/Idle, the instruction being latched in Update-IR. TMS = 1, 0, 0 reaches Shift-DR, where the selected data register shifts in from TDI (TMS low for all bits but the last) while the values captured in Capture-DR shift out on TDO; TMS = 1, 1, 0 returns to idle, a latched output register updating in Update-DR. The Exit and Pause states only navigate. Run-Test/Idle need not be passed between choosing an instruction and using its register, and some instructions act in Run-Test/Idle. Five TCK periods with TMS high reach Test-Logic-Reset from any state.

Debug hardware is a scan chain between the CPU and the peripherals, a break-point unit, and a link between CPU and JTAG. The debugger reads and writes by feeding AVR instructions through the CPU scan chain; the CPU posts results to an I/O location in the link. The break-point unit offers breaks on a program-flow change and on single steps, plus two program-memory and two combined break points, usable as: four program-memory break points; three program plus one data; two program plus two data; two program plus one program break point with mask (range); or two program plus one data break point with mask. A debugger may keep some of these for itself. On-chip debug needs JTAGEN and OCDEN programmed and no lock bits set; setting LB1 or LB2 turns it off so that it cannot open a locked part.

AVR Studio controls execution on parts with on-chip debug, on the in-circuit emulator or on its simulator, at source level (assembly, or C from third-party compilers) and at disassembly level: run, step into or over, step out, run to cursor, stop and reset. Code break points (BREAK instructions) are unlimited; data memory break points number two, or one combined as a masked range.

Programming through JTAG uses only TCK, TMS, TDI and TDO besides the supply pins, and needs no 12 V. It needs JTAGEN programmed and MCUCR's JTD bit at 0. Flash, EEPROM, fuses and lock bits can each be programmed and verified. Lock-bit protection is the same as in parallel programming: with LB1 or LB2 programmed, OCDEN cannot be programmed until a chip erase has been done.

OCDR (I/O address 0x31, data address 0x51) carries bytes from the running program to the debugger. A CPU write sets the internal flag IDRD (I/O debug register dirty); a CPU read returns seven bits of OCDR with IDRD as the top bit; the debugger clears IDRD once it has read the byte. Where OCDR shares an I/O location, it is reached only with OCDEN programmed and the debugger enabling it; otherwise the ordinary I/O register is accessed.

The boundary-scan chain drives and observes the digital I/O pins and the digital side of analog circuits that connect off chip. On a board, every JTAG part is chained TDI to TDO into one long shift register; a tester sets output pins, reads inputs from other parts and compares them with the expected result, testing interconnects through the four TAP signals. The mandatory instructions IDCODE, BYPASS, SAMPLE/PRELOAD and EXTEST and the public AVR_RESET serve board test; IDCODE is the default, so the first data-register scan returns the ID code. Holding the part in reset during test keeps scan data and firmware from interfering; in reset every port output goes high impedance at once, which is why HIGHZ is not needed. Reset comes from pulling RESET low or from AVR_RESET with the reset register set. EXTEST drives the output latches onto the pins as soon as it is loaded, so SAMPLE/PRELOAD should set safe values first; SAMPLE/PRELOAD also snapshots the pins in normal running. JTAGEN programmed and JTD in MCUCR cleared enable the TAP. TCK may run faster than the chip clock, and the chip clock need not run.

Four data registers serve boundary scan: bypass, device identification, reset and the boundary-scan chain. The bypass register is one stage, cleared to 0 on leaving Capture-DR, and shortens the chain when other parts are under test. The reset register holds the part in reset while it holds a 1 (like RESET pulled low); after it clears, the part stays in reset for the reset time-out the clock fuses set. Its output is not latched, so reset acts at once. Because reset tri-states the port pins, it stands in for the missing HIGHZ instruction.

Each bidirectional port pin has a boundary-scan cell with a two-stage shift register serving three signals: OCxn (output control), ODxn (output data) and IDxn (input data). With EXTEST or SAMPLE_PRELOAD in the instruction register the pin's pull-up is disabled.

operation.topic: Port pin signals in the scan chain
operation.text: With no alternate function active, input data is the PINxn value without its synchronizer, output data is the PORT register, output control the data direction bit DDxn; PUExn, the pull-up enable, is on when PUD is 0, DDxn is 0 and PORTxn is 1. Digital alternate functions join outside the scan cell, so the chain reads the real pin level. Analog functions connect straight from pin to analog circuit with no scan cell between, though some digital controls to the analog side are switched off to avoid contention on the pad. With EXTEST or SAMPLE_PRELOAD loaded, the system clock is not driven onto its port pin even with CKOUT programmed, and the boundary scan does not sample the clock.
RESET takes a 5 V active-low reset in normal use and an active-high 12 V level for high-voltage parallel programming. The 5 V reset signal has an observe-only scan cell (RSTT in the chain).
Boundary-scan description language files, which give the order and function of every bit in the boundary-scan register for automatic test generation, exist for these devices.

The MCU can download and upload its own program code through a Flash-resident boot loader, with real read-while-write self-programming. The boot loader may use any data interface and protocol, can write anywhere in Flash including its own section, and so can rewrite or erase itself. Its size is set by fuses, a separate fuse selects the reset vector, and two independent sets of boot lock bits set the protection. A page is a group of Flash bytes used in programming; page organisation does not matter in normal running.

Flash divides into an application section and a boot loader section (BLS), sized by the BOOTSZ fuses and protected by separate lock bits: boot lock bits 0 for the application, boot lock bits 1 for the BLS. SPM only starts a programming operation when executed from the BLS, so boot loader code must live there and can never live in the application section; from the BLS, SPM reaches all of Flash.

Flash also divides into two fixed sections, read-while-write (RWW) and no-read-while-write (NRWW). Erasing or writing a page in RWW leaves NRWW readable; erasing or writing a page in NRWW halts the CPU for the whole operation. The names refer to the section being programmed, not the one being read. During an RWW update, code in RWW must not be read: an LPM, call, jump or interrupt into RWW may leave the software in an unknown state, so interrupts should be disabled or moved to the BLS. The BLS always lies in NRWW. RWWSB in SPMCSR reads 1 while RWW is blocked, and software must clear it before running code there again.

Without a boot loader all of Flash holds application code. The two boot lock bit sets allow: the whole Flash protected from MCU updates; only the BLS protected; only the application section protected; or updates allowed everywhere. Boot lock bits can be set by software and in serial or parallel programming, but only a chip erase clears them. Lock bit mode 2 (write lock) stops SPM programming Flash; mode 3 (read/write lock) stops both (E)LPM reads and SPM writes.

The application enters the boot loader by a jump or call, for instance on a command arriving over the USART or SPI. Alternatively the BOOTRST fuse points the reset vector at the boot loader start, so it runs after every reset and then starts the application once it is loaded. The MCU cannot change its own fuses: once BOOTRST is programmed, only serial or parallel programming can change it back.

SPM commands take their address from the Z-pointer: ZL and ZH in the register file, extended by RAMPZ in I/O space, which exists only where program space exceeds 64 Kbytes (ATmega1284/1284P). The low bits of the program counter select a word within a page and the high bits select which page. Page Erase and Page Write are addressed separately, so the boot loader must give both the same page. Once an operation starts its address is latched and Z is free for other use. LPM addresses Flash by byte and so also uses bit Z0.

Flash is rewritten a page at a time. A page must be erased before it is written from the temporary page buffer, which SPM fills one word at a time, either before Page Erase (fill, erase, write) or between erase and write (erase, fill, write). To change part of a page the rest must be saved, for instance in that buffer, before the erase; filling first allows read-modify-write, while erasing first leaves the old data unreadable during loading. The buffer may be filled in any order. Page Erase and Page Write must address the same page.

With the SPM interrupt enabled, the interrupt stays asserted while SPMEN in SPMCSR is clear, replacing software polling. The interrupt vectors should then be moved to the BLS so that no interrupt reads RWW while it is blocked.

Leaving boot lock bit 11 unprogrammed lets the BLS be rewritten, and a stray write can then destroy the boot loader and any later update. When the boot loader never needs changing, programming BLB11 guards it against software writes.

operation.topic: Keeping the RWW section unread during self-programming
operation.text: Page Erase and Page Write always block reads of RWW, and software itself must keep from addressing it. RWWSB in SPMCSR stays set while RWW is busy. Move the vector table to the BLS or disable interrupts during self-programming, and clear RWWSB by writing RWWSRE before touching RWW afterwards.
An EEPROM write blocks all software Flash programming and also software reads of fuses and lock bits. Software should see EEPE in EECR clear before writing SPMCSR.

operation.topic: Reading fuse and lock bits from software
operation.text: Load Z with the byte's address, set BLBSET and SPMEN in SPMCSR, and execute (E)LPM within three CPU cycles: the byte lands in the destination register. BLBSET and SPMEN clear themselves when the read completes, or if no (E)LPM follows within three cycles or no SPM within four; afterwards (E)LPM behaves normally. Programmed bits read 0 and unprogrammed bits read 1.

operation.topic: Reading the signature row from software
operation.text: Load Z with the signature-row address, set SIGRD and SPMEN in SPMCSR, and execute LPM within three CPU cycles to get the byte. SIGRD and SPMEN clear themselves when the read completes or if no LPM follows within three cycles; LPM then behaves normally.

At low VCC the Flash can be corrupted in two ways: a Flash write needs a minimum voltage, and the CPU can mis-execute instructions when the supply is too low. Any one of these prevents it: program the boot loader lock bits when the boot loader never needs updating; hold RESET active while the supply is too low, with the brown-out detector if its level fits the operating voltage or with an external low-VCC reset circuit (a write in progress at reset still completes if the supply suffices); or keep the core in power-down sleep while VCC is low so that it executes nothing and cannot write SPMCSR.

A minimal boot loader routine writes one page from RAM (pointed to by Y) to Flash (pointed to by Z): Page Erase, re-enable RWW, load a page buffer word by word with SPM, Page Write, re-enable RWW, then an optional read-back compare, and finally waits until RWWSB is clear before returning to RWW code. The SPM helper waits for the previous SPM to finish (SPMEN clear), saves SREG and disables interrupts, waits for any EEPROM write (EEPE) to end, writes SPMCSR and executes SPM, then restores SREG. At least the SPM helper must lie in the boot section, since only NRWW code can run during erase and write; it assumes interrupts are disabled or the vector table is in the boot loader section.
Six lock bits, each left unprogrammed (1) or programmed (0), add the protection in the lock bit protection table. Only the chip erase command returns them to 1.
Four fuse bytes; a programmed fuse reads 0. Chip erase leaves the fuses unchanged. Programming LB1 locks the fuses, so fuses are programmed before lock bits.

Fuse values are latched on entering programming mode, and changes take effect only after leaving it; EESAVE is the exception and acts as soon as it is programmed. In normal mode the fuses are latched at power-up.
A three-byte signature code identifies the device; it sits in its own address space and can be read in serial and parallel mode even on a locked part.

One calibration byte for the internal RC oscillator is stored in the high byte of address 0x000 of the signature space; reset copies it into OSCCAL so the calibrated oscillator starts at the right frequency.

In parallel programming several pins take programming roles (pin name mapping table). XA1 and XA0 pick what a positive pulse on XTAL1 does; the loaded command picks what a pulse on WR or OE does. Pulses are at least 250 ns unless stated otherwise. Pins not used in parallel programming are left floating.

1) Put 4.5 to 5.5 V between VCC and GND. 2) Hold RESET at 0 and toggle XTAL1 six times or more. 3) Set the four Prog_enable pins (PAGEL, XA1, XA0, BS1) to 0000 and wait 100 ns or more. 4) Raise RESET to 11.5 to 12.5 V; any change on the Prog_enable pins within 100 ns of the 12 V edge makes entry fail. 5) Wait 50 µs or more before the first command.

Command and address stay loaded during programming. A command is loaded once for many reads or writes; 0xFF data need not be written after a chip erase (the whole Flash, and the EEPROM unless EESAVE is programmed); the address high byte is loaded only when moving to a new 256-word Flash window or 256-byte EEPROM window, which also holds for signature reads.

Chip erase clears Flash, EEPROM (kept if EESAVE is programmed) and the lock bits, the lock bits only once the program memory is fully erased; fuses are untouched. Flash and EEPROM must be chip-erased before they are reprogrammed. Sequence: XA1, XA0 = 10 (command load); BS1 = 0; DATA = 1000 0000; positive pulse on XTAL1; negative pulse on WR starts the erase and RDY/BSY goes low; wait for RDY/BSY high before the next command.

operation.topic: Programming the Flash in parallel mode
operation.text: Flash is programmed a page at a time through a page buffer. A, load command: XA1, XA0 = 10, BS1 = 0, DATA = 0001 0000, pulse XTAL1. B, address low byte (bits 7..0): XA1, XA0 = 00, BS2, BS1 = 00, DATA = the byte, pulse XTAL1. C, data low byte: XA1, XA0 = 01, DATA = the byte, pulse XTAL1. D, data high byte: BS1 = 1, XA1, XA0 = 01, DATA = the byte, pulse XTAL1. E, latch: BS1 = 1, positive pulse on PAGEL latches the word. F: repeat B to E until the buffer or that page's data is loaded. The low address bits select a word inside a page and the high bits pick which page; with fewer than 256 words per page, the top bits of the address low byte take part in addressing pages at Page Write. G, address high byte (bits 15..8): XA1, XA0 = 00, BS2, BS1 = 01, DATA = the byte, pulse XTAL1. H, address extended high byte (bits 23..16): XA1, XA0 = 00, BS2, BS1 = 10, DATA = the byte, pulse XTAL1. I, program it: BS2, BS1 = 00, negative pulse on WR, RDY/BSY goes low; wait for it to go high. J: repeat B to I until all data is programmed. K, end: XA1, XA0 = 10, DATA = 0000 0000 (no operation), pulse XTAL1, which resets the internal write signals.

operation.topic: Programming the EEPROM in parallel mode
operation.text: EEPROM is also programmed a page at a time through a page buffer. Load command 0001 0001 (A), address high byte (G), address low byte (B), data (C), and latch with a PAGEL pulse (E); repeat address low, data and latch until the buffer is full. Then set BS2, BS1 = 00 and give WR a negative pulse; RDY/BSY goes low, and the next page waits until it is high again.

operation.topic: Reading the Flash and EEPROM in parallel mode
operation.text: Flash: load command 0000 0010, then the extended, high and low address bytes; with OE = 0 and BS1 = 0 the word's low byte appears on DATA, with BS1 = 1 the high byte; set OE = 1 to finish. EEPROM: load command 0000 0011, the high and low address bytes, then OE = 0 and BS1 = 0 put the byte on DATA; set OE = 1 to finish.

operation.topic: Programming fuses and lock bits in parallel mode
operation.text: Fuses: load command 0100 0000 and the data low byte (a 0 bit programs that fuse, a 1 erases it). For the low byte give WR a negative pulse; for the high byte first set BS2, BS1 = 01, and for the extended byte BS2, BS1 = 10; wait for RDY/BSY high, then return BS2, BS1 to 00. Lock bits: load command 0010 0000 and the data low byte (a 0 bit programs that lock bit), pulse WR low and wait for RDY/BSY high. Once LB mode 3 is set, no external programming mode can program the boot lock bits. Only chip erase clears lock bits.

operation.topic: Reading fuses, lock bits, signature and calibration in parallel mode
operation.text: After command 0000 0100 and OE = 0, BS2, BS1 select what DATA shows (0 means programmed): 00 the fuse low byte, 11 the fuse high byte, 10 the extended fuse byte, 01 the lock bits; set OE = 1 to finish. Signature: command 0000 1000, address low byte 0x00 to 0x02, OE = 0 and BS1 = 0 put the byte on DATA. Calibration byte: command 0000 1000, address low byte 0x00, OE = 0 and BS1 = 1.

Flash and EEPROM can be programmed over a serial bus of SCK, MOSI (input) and MISO (output) while RESET is held at GND. After RESET goes low the Programming Enable instruction must run before any program or erase operation. Not every package uses the SPI peripheral's own pins for serial programming.

In serial mode an EEPROM write erases the location itself as part of its self-timed cycle, so no chip erase is needed first. Chip erase sets every Flash and EEPROM location to 0xFF. A valid clock, as the CKSEL fuses select, must run. SCK low and high times must each exceed 2 CPU clock cycles for fck below 12 MHz, and 3 CPU clock cycles for fck of 12 MHz and above. Input data is clocked in on the rising edge of SCK, and output data out on the falling edge.

1) Power up with RESET and SCK at 0; if the programmer cannot hold SCK low during power-up, pulse RESET high for at least two CPU clocks after SCK is 0. 2) Wait 20 ms or more, then send Programming Enable on MOSI. 3) When in step, the second byte (0x53) echoes back while the third byte goes out; all four bytes are sent either way, and without the echo RESET gets a positive pulse and Programming Enable is sent again. 4) Flash is written a page at a time: each byte goes into a page buffer with Load Program Memory Page and the seven low address bits, low data byte before high byte for each address; Write Program Memory Page with address bits 15..8 then stores it. Load Extended Address Byte sets the top address byte first; it holds until sent again, so it is needed only for the first page and at each 64K-word boundary. Without RDY/BSY polling, wait tWD_FLASH before the next page; touching the interface before the write ends can corrupt it. 5) EEPROM is written a byte at a time with address and data in one Write instruction; each location erases itself first. Without polling, wait tWD_EEPROM before the next byte. 0xFF need not be written to an erased part. 6) Read instructions return any location on MISO; for Flash, Load Extended Address Byte supplies the top address byte, held as in step 4. 7) Raise RESET to start normal running. 8) To power off, set RESET to 1, then remove VCC.
The serial programming interface follows the SPI slave timing in the SPI timing characteristics. MOSI and MISO carry the most significant bit first.

JTAG programming needs control of TCK, TMS, TDI and TDO only, not of the reset or clock pins. JTAGEN must be programmed (as shipped) and JTD in MCUCR cleared. If JTD is set, forcing the external reset low clears JTD after two chip clocks and frees the JTAG pins for programming, so the pins can be port pins in normal running and still allow in-system JTAG programming; this does not work for boundary scan or on-chip debug, which need the pins dedicated. TCK must stay below the chip's maximum frequency during programming; the system clock prescaler cannot divide TCK down. Shift registers shift least significant bit first.

operation.topic: JTAG page load and page read
operation.text: PROG_PAGELOAD alternates low and high bytes on each Update-DR, starting with the low byte after the instruction is entered; the program counter advances before each low byte except the first, so the first word lands at the address set with PROG_COMMANDS and loading the last word does not step into the next page. PROG_PAGEREAD alternates low and high bytes on each Capture-DR, starting with the low byte; the program counter advances after every high byte, the first included, so reading starts at the set address and the last word of a page steps into the next page.

Programming uses four data registers: reset, programming enable, programming command and Flash data byte. The part must be reset through the reset register before entering programming mode. A 1 in the reset register acts like RESET held low; after release the part stays in reset for the time-out the clock fuses set; the output is not latched, so reset is immediate.

A 16-bit register compared with the programming enable signature 0b1010_0011_0111_0000 (0xA370); JTAG programming is enabled while they match. Power-on reset clears it, and it should be cleared on leaving programming mode.
A 15-bit register that shifts programming commands in and the previous command's result, if any, out. The commands are in the JTAG programming instruction table.

An 8-bit scan chain plus an 8-bit temporary register; it loads a whole Flash page buffer before Page Write, or reads back Flash, with only the data shifted, since a state machine drives the Flash controls and watches its strobes. The state machine runs on TCK. With eight bits shifted per byte, the TCK edges spent moving through the TAP states give it enough clocks; if fewer bits are shifted between Update-DR states during page load, stay in Run-Test/Idle long enough that at least 11 TCK cycles separate each Update-DR.

Instruction codes 1a, 1b and so on are rows of the JTAG programming instruction table. Enter programming mode: AVR_RESET with 1 shifted into the reset register, then PROG_ENABLE with 0b1010_0011_0111_0000. Leave it: PROG_COMMANDS, no-operation 11a, PROG_ENABLE with 0b0000_0000_0000_0000, then AVR_RESET with 0. Chip erase: PROG_COMMANDS, 1a, then poll with 1b or wait tWLRH_CE. Flash and EEPROM must be chip-erased before programming.

Word by word: PROG_COMMANDS; 2a; 2b, 2c, 2d for the address; 2e, 2f, 2g for the data; repeat address low and data for every word of that page; 2h writes it; poll 2i or wait tWLRH; repeat from the extended address for each page. Faster with PROG_PAGELOAD: PROG_COMMANDS; 2a; 2b, 2c, 2d with PCWORD = 0; enter PROG_PAGELOAD and shift in a whole page byte by byte from the LSB of the first word to the MSB of the last, each Update-DR storing the byte and advancing the program counter; back to PROG_COMMANDS; 2h; poll 2i or wait tWLRH; repeat per page.

Word by word: PROG_COMMANDS; 3a; 3b, 3c, 3d for the address; 3e reads the word; repeat. Faster with PROG_PAGEREAD: PROG_COMMANDS; 3a; 3b, 3c, 3d with PCWORD = 0; enter PROG_PAGEREAD and shift out a whole page (or the whole Flash) from the LSB of the first word to the MSB of the last. Capture-DR both captures the data and advances the program counter, and it comes before Shift-DR, so the first byte out is already valid. Return to PROG_COMMANDS and repeat per page.

operation.topic: EEPROM, fuses and lock bits through JTAG
operation.text: EEPROM write: PROG_COMMANDS; 4a; 4b and 4c for the address; 4d and 4e for each byte of that page; 4f writes it; poll 4g or wait tWLRH. EEPROM read: 5a, 5b, 5c, then 5d per byte. PROG_PAGELOAD and PROG_PAGEREAD do not work on the EEPROM. Fuses: 6a, then for each byte load the data (a 0 programs, a 1 unprograms), write it and poll or wait tWLRH. Lock bits: 7a, 7b with the data (a 0 programs, a 1 leaves the bit), 7c, then poll 7d or wait tWLRH. Reading: 8a, then 8f reads all four bytes, or 8b to 8e read one. Signature: 9a, then 9b with address 0x00, 0x01 and 0x02 in turn, each followed by 9c. Calibration: 10a, 10b with address 0x00, then 10c.
The highest clock frequency depends on VCC: 4 MHz at 1.8 V, 10 MHz at 2.7 V and 20 MHz from 4.5 V to 5.5 V, rising linearly from 1.8 V to 2.7 V and from 2.7 V to 4.5 V.

The typical characteristics are characterisation data and are not tested in production. Supply currents were taken with every I/O pin an input with its pull-up on, clocked from a sine-wave generator whose output swings rail to rail. For the Active and Idle graphs every PRR bit was set, turning the I/O modules off, and the analog comparator was off. Power-down current is the same whatever clock source is selected.

operation.topic: Typical characteristics: what sets the supply current
operation.text: Current rises with VCC, clock frequency, pin loading and toggle rate, the code being run and ambient temperature; VCC and frequency matter most. Parts were measured above their tested clock limits, yet only the frequency of the ordering code is guaranteed. The watchdog timer draws the difference between Power-down current with it on and with it off.

operation.topic: Supply current of the I/O modules
operation.text: In Active and Idle mode each I/O module left on in the Power Reduction Register adds to the supply current. Its share is given both in microamps at three VCC and clock points and as a percentage of the external-clock Active or Idle current, and the percentage carries over to other VCC and clock settings.

The graphs to 105 °C cover ATmega164PA, 324PA, 644PA and 1284P and are characterisation data, not production tests. Every I/O pin was an input with its pull-up on, the clock a rail-to-rail sine wave, and for Active and Idle current every PRR bit was set and the analog comparator off. Power-down current does not depend on the clock source, and the watchdog current is the difference between Power-down with and without the watchdog.

Every device runs to 20 MHz from 1.8 V to 5.5 V within the speed grades. Codes ending -AU, -PU, -MU, -MCH and -CU are for -40 °C to 85 °C; ATmega164PA, 324PA, 644PA and 1284P also come as -AN, -PN and -MN for -40 °C to 105 °C. A trailing R is tape and reel. The 44MC and 49C2 packages are offered for ATmega164A, 164PA, 324A and 324PA only.
